articles.body: For Cleveland Guardians fans, José Ramírez is known as one of the most consistent and electrifying hitters in Major League Baseball. The Dominican third baseman and six-time Silver Slugger award winner has made a name for himself with clutch performances, loyalty with Cleveland, and a relentless work ethic. Away from the diamond, however, Ramírez lives a much quieter life that is centered around family and the woman who was a part of his journey long before the spotlight came.From hometown romance to a long-lasting marriageRamírez shares his life with Rosedith Almonte, his long-time partner, who grew up in the same town as him in the Dominican Republic. Their relationship started years before Ramírez signed his first professional contract, making a teenage romance a long-lasting marriage. As the MLB star's career has grown, bringing All-Star selections, lucrative contracts, and endorsement deals, Almonte has been a constant presence behind the scenes. Jose Ramirez and Rosedith Almonte both grew up in Bani, Dominican Republic, where their relationship was said to have begun even in their teenage years. What began as a high school romance eventually turned into a long-term relationship as Ramirez worked his way up the ranks of professional baseball. While Ramirez was grinding through the Cleveland Guardians' minor-league system after being signed as an international prospect in 2009, Almonte was focusing on her education. She later went on to study in the United States, where she attended Cuyahoga Community College in Cleveland and pursued creative work in digital design.Unlike many of the partners of professional athletes, Almonte has avoided the public spotlight for the most part. She does not have a very public presence on social media but does share the occasional family moment, celebration, and glimpse of life during the MLB season.Family life, endorsements, and the life Ramirez created off the fieldJosé Ramírez and Rosedith Almonte have three children: Isabella, Jose Jr., and Isaell, and the family divides time between Cleveland during the MLB season and the Dominican Republic during the offseason, staying connected to his roots. Off the field, Ramirez has also developed an expanding financial framework through contracts and brand partnerships. The Guardians star signed a $175 million contract extension in 2022 for seven years, to ensure his future with the franchise through 2028. In addition to his salary, he has endorsements for baseball gear, training equipment, and sportswear brands.Despite the financial success, Ramirez has repeatedly emphasized giving back. He has provided funds for upgrades on youth baseball fields in Bani, and regularly invests in community programs in the Dominican Republic and Cleveland. articles.title: Guardians X-factor that means everything for do-or-die Game 5 vs. White Sox
articles.summary: The playoffs is not the time for making conservative plays; at least that’s what the Cleveland Guardians must have been thinking. After all, they headed to t...
articles.body:
The playoffs is not the time for making conservative plays; at least that's what the Cleveland Guardians must have been thinking. After all, they headed to the road in the ALDS against the Chicago White Sox down 2-0 and had to win at all costs to keep their season alive — even at the cost of their pitching staff's freshness .

In Game 4, the Guardians had to send out Gavin Williams , their starter for Game 5 and one of their best pitchers, to close things out — having him throw 18 pitches to send the series to a do-or-die contest with a 9-5 victory. Before Williams, it looks as though the heavy workload was getting to their best reliever in Cade Smith, who's pitched in all four games of the ALDS thus far. Smith allowed a home run and a walk during his last time out on the mound, which necessitated Williams' relief appearance.

As pointed out by Jon Morosi of MLB Network, the pitch count for the Guardians' hurlers are undoubtedly going to play a part in Game 5 — being a major X-factor that could prove to be the difference between a trip to St. Petersburg for Game 1 of the ALCS against the Tampa Bay Rays and an early exit from the postseason.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Smith has thrown 67 pitches in this series, including 31 in Game 4. Will he be fresh enough to come in relief yet again in Game 5? Foster Griffin, who will be available off the pen in Game 5, threw 53 pitches back on Wednesday in Game 3.

Will Parker Messick, the Guardians' starter who struggled in Game 4, be available just in case the team needs him to? Or has Cleveland burnt their pitchers out enough just to survive?

Only time will tell whether or not Stephen Vogt made the right decisions. But one thing's for sure: he prioritized the Guardians' survival, and they're still alive and kicking, which means that their gambit, up until this point, has worked.

articles.title: Ranking Yankees OF Trent Grisham's Top 10 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: After slugging 34 home runs during the 2025 season, Trent Grisham returned to the New York Yankees when he accepted a one-year, $22.025 million qualifying offer last winter.
articles.body:
After slugging 34 home runs during the 2025 season, Trent Grisham returned to the New York Yankees when he accepted a one-year, $22.025 million qualifying offer last winter.

The 29-year-old failed to match his career year, hitting .211/.308/.395 for a 95 OPS+ with 18 home runs, 59 RBI and 0.6 WAR in 121 games, but he should still draw plenty of interest in free agency.

His age, on-base ability and power in a market that is thin on center field options could still land him a multi-year deal, and his defensive profile means there won't be clear overlap with the market for corner bats like Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki.

A reunion with the Yankees this time around is unlikely, with Spencer Jones emerging alongside Cody Bellinger and Aaron Judge to form next year's outfield, so what jersey will Grisham be wearing in 2027?

Ahead is a rundown of his top 10 speculative suitors.

With Mike Trout, Josh Lowe, Jose Siri and rookie standout Wade Meckler, the Angels have enough in-house talent to stand pat in the outfield. At the same time, Grisham feels like the sort of mid-tier veteran they have targeted in years past, and signing him would allow Trout to return to a corner spot.

The Padres had a revolving door in left field for much of the season before a platoon of Dustin Harris (100 PA, 120 OPS+, 0.9 WAR) and Samad Taylor (175 PA, 124 OPS+, 0.8 WAR) proved to be surprisingly productive. They could run it back with that tandem, but Grisham would provide a more established alternative, and San Diego is plenty familiar with his game.

How many more chances will Evan Carter get to be an everyday center fielder? The 24-year-old was a 1.9-WAR player in 2026, but it was almost solely on the strength of his defense, as he hit .194/.288/.315 for a 76 OPS+ over 455 plate appearances. At this point, he looks more like a glove-only fourth outfielder than the impactful all-around talent he hinted at early in his career.

Disappointing seasons from Dylan Beavers (104 G, 93 OPS+, -0.5 WAR) and Tyler O'Neill (85 G, 92 OPS+, 0.5 WAR) give the Orioles plenty of room to potentially upgrade alongside Colton Cowser in the outfield. The question is how far down the shopping list that will be when pitching is the clear No. 1 priority.

The Blue Jays have already been linked to Seiya Suzuki, and Randy Arozarena fits into a similar bucket as a right-handed hitting, middle-of-the-order corner outfielder. Grisham is unquestionably a tier below those two in terms of expected impact, but he could be a viable fallback plan if they whiff on those top targets.

Projected OF: LF Casey Schmitt, CF Drew Gilbert, RF Jung Hoo Lee

The unmitigated disaster that was the Harrison Bader signing could scare the Giants away from another high-profile addition to the outfield, but it's a group that is far from settled.

Drew Gilbert posted an .812 OPS in 142 plate appearances over the final two months of the season, and he is a plus defender in center field (3 DRS, 5 OAA), so he is a viable in-house candidate if they decide to focus on pitching.

Otherwise, Grisham has the speed and defensive reputation to be a good fit in spacious Oracle Park, and Gilbert could still factor into the starting mix with Casey Schmitt best used as a first baseman or designated hitter.

Each Team's Biggest Roster Hole to Fix in Offseason ⚾

The 10 Greatest MLB Divisional Series Upsets 😮

Projected OF: LF Isaac Collins, CF Kyle Isbel, RF Jac Caglianone

The emergence of Jac Caglianone gives the Royals one clear answer in the outfield after they entered the 2026 season with three genuine question marks, but they could still use an upgrade at the other two spots.

The Royals ranked 28th in OPS for left fielders (.660) and 24th in OPS for center fielders (.658), and the returning trio of Kyle Isbel, Isaac Collins and John Rave probably all profile best as fourth outfielders on a contending team.

Grisham's asking price will be the determining factor in whether the Royals are viable contenders for his services, but he looks like a solid buy-low target to potentially upgrade one of their biggest roster holes.

Projected OF: LF Michael Arroyo, CF Julio Rodríguez, RF Dominic Canzone

Ideally, the Mariners would find a way to retain Randy Arozarena, who was easily their most productive hitter in 2026, though that will likely require a nine-figure commitment as he is arguably the top bat on the market.

They could also opt to go young, using Michael Arroyo in left field after he went 13-for-35 with two doubles and one home run in 15 games as a September call-up, and he has a long track record of production in the minors.

However, Grisham would give them an established everyday option, a viable platoon partner for the right-handed hitting Arroyo and a capable backup for Julio Rodríguez in center field. That last part is important, assuming they decline a $9 million club option on Victor Robles as expected.

Projected OF: LF JJ Bleday, CF Dane Myers, RF Héctor Rodríguez

Aside from a strong season from scrapheap pickup JJ Bleday (105 OPS+, 24 HR, 1.2 WAR), the Reds outfield was sorely lacking in impact production in 2026, and that has been a recurring theme in recent years.

Dane Myers had a 101 OPS+ over 334 plate appearances, but with 19 extra-base hits, a .377 slugging percentage and an OPS that was 99 points higher against left-handed pitching, he is a straight platoon option.

That actually makes the Grisham fit even stronger, as he could pair with Myers in center field and give the team a potential insurance policy while young guys like Héctor Rodríguez and Carlos Jorge work to establish themselves as big league options.

Projected OF: LF Taylor Trammell, CF Lucas Spence, RF Cam Smith

Cam Smith started 139 games in right field for the Astros last season, but left field and center field were as "by-committee" as any team in baseball while they searched for answers.

They ultimately used 12 different starting left fielders and eight different starting center fielders, with no one reaching 40 starts at either position.

Lucas Spence showed enough down the stretch to get a long look this spring, but they can't enter another season hoping the likes of Taylor Trammell, Jake Meyers, Joey Loperfido and Brice Matthews can absorb everyday playing time.

Expect them to cast a wide net in their search for outfield help, and their center field need specifically helps put Grisham high on their list of potential targets.

articles.title: World Series champion says potential MLB lockout could 'absolutely' cause cancelled games next season
articles.summary: World Series champion Nick Swisher said games could "absolutely" be missed next season as MLB and the players association remain far apart on the thought of a salary cap.
articles.body: In a normal year, most MLB teams would already be looking toward next year at this point in the season, as only a few teams remain alive. But what does next season even look like? Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association are all but guaranteed to have a lockout beginning Dec. 1 , as both sides have diametrically opposed positions on a salary cap. The owners are pushing hard to implement a salary cap, while the players are vehemently opposed. World Series champion Nick Swisher said that games could "absolutely" be missed next season due to a stalemate between the two sides. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Absolutely, because just like yourself as me, is all of a sudden, you hear the players association speaking this language and the commissioner's office is speaking this language. I immediately knew out of the gate. Plus, just knowing a little bit more under the hood about the last couple of collective bargaining agreements, right?" Swisher told OutKick in a recent interview. The former New York Yankees star noted that Tony Clark is no longer the head of the MLBPA after resigning in February and that Bruce Meyer, who took over for Clark, will want everyone to know how he does business. Swisher said he hopes both sides go to the negotiating table in good faith. "When you get people going to the negotiation table, you're hoping that everyone's trying to go to negotiate a fair deal. You're hoping that both sides aren't trying to go to the negotiation table to win. Because if that's the case, we're in a lot of trouble. Because we're really, really far apart from each other right now, and the last thing we wanna do is slow this train down," Swisher said. Swisher said baseball is "absolutely crushing" right now, with revenue and attendance both up, going so far as to say that the game has never been in a better place. Yet, having spent 12 seasons in the big leagues, he understands just how tough the union is. "Pretty much all other sports are very salary cap-based, and that's kind of been the one thing for the players association and the players union. It's one of the strongest unions in the world for a reason, because they stand up for each other. And I was part of that before. I know the bond, I know the brothership, and, listen, it's a tough union," Swisher said. WILL MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL STILL LOCK PLAYERS OUT AFTER 2026 POSTSEASON PROVES OWNERS WRONG? Swisher, like the rest of the baseball world, hopes the two sides can reach an agreement before any games are lost . "I think at the end of the day, man, I'm praying that everything gets itself back on track come the end of the season because I wouldn't wanna slow this train down, man. It's moving too fast right now and we got too many things going on well in our game to be slowing it down right now," Swisher said. BASEBALL OR BABY? During the Division Series, two prominent players were forced to make an impossible decision: Miss their child's birth or leave their team during the postseason to attend the milestone event? About an hour before the San Diego Padres faced the Milwaukee Brewers with their season on the line, All-Star closer Mason Miller went on the paternity list to attend the birth of his child. The Padres won Game 3 and staved off elimination in his absence. New York Yankees starting pitcher Max Fried, on the other hand, said that despite his girlfriend being ready to give birth at any moment, he would pitch in Game 3 no matter what. The Yankees lost the game, so Fried is now free to support his girlfriend for the foreseeable future. Swisher, a father of two children , said he was fortunate to avoid the dilemma Miller and Fried faced . "I was very blessed that I had one child that was born at the beginning of the season and one child that was born in the middle of the season. So, I didn't get presented with this situation where both of these individuals are put in," Swisher said. LEGENDARY SPORTS AGENT WARNS MLB LOCKOUT WOULD BE 'REMARKABLY SELF-DESTRUCTIVE' WITH CBA SET TO EXPIRE "It's hard for me to say that as a father now of two beautiful young girls that I wouldn't want to be there for the birth of my daughter. But once again, I was never put in that position." Having played in numerous postseason games, the former All-Star outfielder said it would have been difficult to miss those opportunities . "At the end of the day, I will tell you this, it's not as often as you think that you get to compete for championships. And for myself, I played in a bunch of playoff games, and we had one great championship run. And it would be really hard for me also to say that I missed out on any of that as well," Swisher said. While it would be difficult to miss a postseason game, the 45-year-old said he couldn't reconcile missing the birth of one of his children. "For myself, at the end of the day, I've never been presented with something like that, so, I really wouldn't even know how to answer that because if I missed the birth of my daughters, either one of them. I feel like that would always bother me," Swisher said. "That would, I would just like – I wasn't there for you. And as a father, that's the one thing that you wanna do is you always wanna be there for your children. So, I can't blame Mason, I can't blame Max." Swisher praised Yankees equipment manager Rob Cucuzza and the entire clubhouse staff for their work. "At the end of the day, I think the unsung heroes are the clubhouse guys, right? The clubhouse, you know, people that, that clean our underwear, right? That wash our jerseys, right, that are up at 4 o'clock in the morning, just unpacking our bags, getting ourselves ready for the next day's worth of work," Swisher, who spoke on behalf of PAYDAY to highlight the low-key legends who helped shape his career, said. "If you don't have those people, if you don't have the engine of your organization, you're not gonna be any good. And the fact that we are so blessed to have someone in New York who does that, who does just that, has an amazing job."

articles.title: Latest World Series 2026 Predictions from MLB Fans, Experts amid Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: Five MLB teams still have a mathematic chance of winning the 2026 World Series.
articles.body:
Five MLB teams still have a mathematic chance of winning the 2026 World Series.

So, it's just 20 percent chances all around, right?

Nope. Not according to...well, just about anyone you ask. From oddsmakers to experts, everyone sees favorites in this field, whether that's an actual favorite or maybe a favorite sleeper.

Before the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago White Sox square off in Saturday's win-or-go-home Game 5 of their ALDS series, let's see what number-crunchers of all kinds think is about to happen.

Who Likes L.A. To Win a Third Straight Title?

Plenty of folks are backing the Los Angeles Dodgers, which makes sense given the talent they've assembled and the achievements they've already realized. Remember, this group claimed both of the past two championships and has since added two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, three-time All-Star closer Edwin Díaz and four-time All-Star outfielder Kyle Tucker.

MLB on Fox's Dontrelle Willis backed the Dodgers for "that rotation, timely hitting, and most important, experience." His colleague, David Ortiz, also took the Dodgers, noting simply, "We've been watching the Dodgers whooping everybody every year, man, and I still don't get enough of it."

The Athletic's Austin Green also backed L.A., opining that the club "just won 100 games while appearing to be in second gear for most of the season." Rotoworld's Matthew Pouliot went L.A., too, saying that improved performance from the bullpen has removed "their biggest weakness."

Experts still aren't overwhelmingly taking the Dodgers the way the oddsmakers say they probably should, but the two-time champs aren't hurting for support.

If the Dodgers Aren't Favorites, Who Is?

Again, oddsmakers and experts are not aligned on the outcome of this MLB season. The Dodgers might have the best odds to pull this off, but the majority of experts are propping up two other teams.

The Milwaukee Brewers, for instance, claimed 56 percent of the vote when The Athletic polled "more than 20...MLB experts" before the playoffs started. For Dennis Lin, the decision came down to Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski being "the freakiest pitching talent" in the sport, and the team being "due to break through in late October."

Things were even simpler for The Athletic's Cody Stavenhagen, who noted that "this year's version (of the Brewers) simply looks like the most well-rounded team there is." Rotoworld's Eric Samulski rationed his pick of the Brewers by writing their "consistency...will win the day here."

In that aformentioned Athletic poll, the Tampa Bay Rays were the second-most popular pick with 24 percent of the vote. Chad Jennings opined that Tampa Bay's "style of play is going to be too disruptive for our expectations." Will Sammon also crowned the Rays, calling them "one of the league's best teams all season" and noting they "got better at the trade deadline."

articles.title: New MLB Rumors on A's Executive Search, Top Candidates from Phillies and Red Sox
articles.summary: A strong contender has reportedly emerged in the Athletics' search for a new president of baseball operations.
articles.body:
A strong contender has reportedly emerged in the Athletics' search for a new president of baseball operations.

According to ESPN's Jeff Passan , Boston Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith is a "top candidate" for the job, while St. Louis Cardinals assistant GM Rob Cerfolio is expected to stay put.

Passan also reported that the A's offered their president of baseball ops position to former Philadelphia Phillies general manager Sam Fuld, but Fuld turned it down and decided to remain as the Phillies' president of business operations.

Each Team's Biggest Roster Hole to Fix in Offseason ⚾

The Athletics' lead baseball executive job became available in August when they fired David Forst after he had served as general manager since 2016.

The A's have not reached the playoffs since 2020, which marked the last of three consecutive trips to the postseason.

While the team showed some signs of improvement last season with a 76-86 record after winning 69 games in 2024 and 50 games in 2023, the Athletics took a step back in 2026.

With a 64-98 mark, the A's finished fourth in a very winnable American League West, as the Houston Astros took the division with only an 81-81 record.

Formerly located in Oakland, the Athletics have played the past two seasons in Sacramento as they await the construction of their new ballpark in Las Vegas, which is expected to be ready for the 2028 season.

The A's have some talented pieces in place, especially offensively in the form of Nick Kurtz, Shea Langeliers, Jacob Wilson, Tyler Soderstrom and Henry Bolte.

However, the Athletics are lacking on the pitching end and could use a top exec capable of acquiring and developing pitchers.

Smith could potentially be the guy, as Boston's assistant GM was formerly part of the Tampa Bay Rays' front office, and few teams are better known for their pitching development than the Rays.

articles.title: 2026 NLCS Preview: Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Milwaukee Brewers
articles.summary: It’s a rematch of last year’s NLCS when the Dodgers swept in four, only this time Milwaukee has The Miz in Cy Young form
articles.body:
It felt inevitable even in the early stages of the season that the two best teams in MLB would be on a collision course for a seismic encounter in the NLCS. The Brewers and Dodgers were the only two teams to finish with at least 100 wins, and by the time both teams jumped out to comfortable leads atop their respective divisions by mid-July, you could sense we were destined for a rematch of last season's NLCS. It should be a far more competitive series than last October, when rampant Dodgers squad swept the Brewers by holding Milwaukee to just one run in each of the four games.

There's no easing into this series — all signs are pointing to a dream matchup of Tarik Skubal vs. Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1, pitting the two-time defending AL Cy Young against this season's presumptive NL Cy Young winner. There was a not insignificant chance that the two aces could have shared a rotation, Milwaukee showing legitimate interest right up until the Dodgers swooped in and acquired Skubal from the Tigers at the deadline. Los Angeles has also tabbed 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto to start Game 2 while the Brewers have yet to select a starter beyond Game 1.

This year's Dodgers remains the juggernaut they've been during this World Series-winning run, but make no mistake, this is a young Brewers squad with an extra year of experience under their belts and the hunger to avenge last year's sweep and make it to their first World Series since their one and only appearance in 1982.

Regular season record: 100-62 (1st, NL West)

This is just as complete a Dodgers team as the one who secured back-to-back World Series titles, Los Angeles keeping their championship core largely intact while making a Cy Young-sized upgrade to the starting rotation. Their offense placed second in MLB behind the Cubs in wRC+ (111) and fWAR (26.9) and is a blend of contact and power, their .257 team batting average and .424 slugging also second-best in MLB. Their starting rotation was tops in the Majors in fWAR (18.7) and second behind the Yankees in ERA (3.43) and FIP (3.69), the group of Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow posing comfortably the highest ceiling of any starting staff in the land. The biggest improvement over last year is their bullpen, which ranked second in MLB in strikeout rate (26.2-percent) and third in FIP (3.67).

The Dodgers advanced past the Braves pretty handily despite Shohei Ohtani remaining mostly absent for the series. It was part of a protracted slump to end the year for the four-time MVP, Ohtani mustering just a 72 wRC+ in September and a 106 mark in the second half. His last home run was on August 18th, the downturn in form likely the result of left knee and right biceps injuries that convinced the Dodgers to remove him from the rotation to DH full time in early July. He went 2-for-13 in the NLDS and will have his streak of three straight NL MVPs snapped by Pete Crow-Armstrong.

Also largely absent from the NLDS were Mookie Betts and Andy Pages. Betts got red-hot to end the regular season but couldn't carry that into the series against the Braves, where he had a 75 wRC+ in 17 plate appearances. Pages established himself as one of the game's premier center fielders this year and last, but was only good for a 77 wRC+ in 15 plate appearances.

Instead, the onus was on Max Muncy, Freddie Freeman, and Kyle Tucker to carry the load against Atlanta. Ever-reliable postseason performer Max Muncy led the way with three home runs and three RBIs to extend his lead atop the franchise postseason home run list to 19. Freeman hit a pair of home runs and drove in a pair against his former team to earn a 174 wRC+ while Tucker batted .333 with a 151 wRC+.

The Dodgers provided a blueprint for how they might deploy their four-headed rotation monster of Skubal, Yamamoto, Snell, and Glasnow with each pitcher making one start in the NLDS. With Skubal and Yamamoto already lined up for the first two games, I imagine Snell and Glasnow will start Games 3 and 4, respectively, based on rest.

Skubal pitched to a 2.61 ERA and 2.36 FIP in ten regular season starts for LA and allowed a run on two hits and two walks with seven strikeouts in six innings in the Dodgers' Game 1 win over the Braves. Yamamoto was even better in Game 3, holding Atlanta to a run on four hits and a walk with ten strikeouts in seven innings following a brilliant regular season in which he went 14-9 in 28 starts with a 2.53 ERA, 3.33 FIP, and 182 strikeouts in 185 innings. Snell was limited to just nine regular season starts in another injury-plagues season, but was dominant to the tune of a 1.90 ERA and 1.72 FIP without giving up a home run in 42.2 innings. He started their lone loss of the NLDS, lasting just 3.2 innings in Game 2 after allowing a run on three hits and five walks. Like Snell, Glasnow was largely unavailable in the regular season, making just 13 starts with a 3.53 ERA and 2.74 FIP, but he helped seal the series in Atlanta by pitching 4.2 innings of one-run ball on one hit and five walks with five strikeouts in the decisive Game 4.

Often the one shaky unit of their playoff runs, the Dodgers bullpen has looked far more settled this postseason. Edwin Díaz returned from a disastrous regular season that saw him demoted from the closer role and suffer elbow and neck injuries to make three scoreless appearances and secure two saves against the Braves. Roki Sasaki, Brock Stewart, and Alex Vesia didn't allow a run in their combined five innings of relief while Edgardo Henriquez's fastball has touched as high as 104 mph. Only Tanner Scott struggled, allowing two runs in 2.2 innings, but he still struck out four of the 11 batters he faced.

Regular season record: 103-59 (1st, NL Central)

The Brewers were the class of MLB, pacing the league with 103 wins. They are what every team aspires to be, blending a cutting edge analytics department with robust player development successes to both produce homegrown cornerstone talent and squeeze as much surplus value out of every player who joins the organization — proof that you do not need a salary cap to make small market teams competitive.

Their offense remained remarkably consistent relative to last year. In 2025, they posted a .257 average, .736 OPS, 166 home runs, a 107 wRC+, and 28.4 fWAR. In 2026, they posted a .257 average, .743 OPS, 154 home runs, a 107 wRC+, and 26.1 fWAR, their offense ranking third right behind the Dodgers in wRC+ and fWAR. Their starting pitching took a big step forward as you might expect when led by a historic campaign from The Miz, the unit finishing fourth in MLB in FIP (3.73) and fWAR (15.6) and fifth in ERA (3.61). The bullpen remained an undeniable strength as it does every year, placing in the top-four in ERA (3.40) and FIP (3.70).

The Brewers were led by ascending superstar Jackson Chourio, who became the all-time franchise leader with five postseason home runs at only 22 years old. Despite just a 73 wRC+ in the series overall, he hit the game-tying two-run homer in Game 1 and the walk-off RBI single with two strikes and two outs off Padres closer Mason Miller in Game 2. He batted .291 with 25 home runs and a 130 wRC+ in the regular season and drove in six in just four games against San Diego.

Their most consistent contributor against the Padres was William Contreras, who went 6-for-16 with two home runs, two RBIs, and a 225 wRC+. Christian Yelich was 5-for-14 with a 162 wRC+ while Jake Bauers and Sal Frelick were on-base machines in that series. Brice Turang, Garrett Mitchell, Joey Ortiz, and Cooper Pratt were all above average by wRC+ during the regular season but none of that quartet did much of anything in the NLDS. If Turang in particular can find his swing after posting a 6 wRC+ in 18 PAs, you'd like their chances a lot more against an LA starting rotation that's in a league above the Padres.

If the Brewers are going to have any chance of advancing to the World Series, it's going to come down to pitching, specifically Jacob Misiorowski. He will likely run away with the NL Cy Young after leading MLB in ERA (1.80), FIP (2.17), strikeouts (252) and fWAR (6.6). He allowed two runs on four hits and a walk with six strikeouts in four innings in the Brewers' Game 1 victory, and in all likelihood will have to start twice and probably make a relief appearance against the Dodgers. He struck out nine in five innings of two-run ball in Game 3 of last year's NLCS against LA.

The quality of options in the rotation after him thins out significantly with Robert Gasser, Logan Henderson, and Dustin May each making one start in the NLDS. Henderson pitched to a 2.47 ERA and 3.32 FIP in 18 regular season starts, the rookie holding the Padres to two runs on two hits and three walks in five innings of a Game 2 walk-off win. Gasser posted a 3.87 ERA and 4.23 FIP in 20 regular seasons starts and held San Diego to a run on three hits and a walk in four innings of the series-clinching Game 4 win. May is the clear black sheep of the bunch, struggling mightily in ten starts after joining from the Cardinals at the deadline and getting tagged for two runs on three hits and two walks of a Game 3 loss.

In my opinion, the X-factor of this series will be the Brewers bullpen, who was taxed heavily in their four games against San Diego, yet have still posted the second-lowest bullpen ERA of any playoff team at 1.80. I expect Milwaukee to continue to lean on the high leverage, high velocity dual threat of Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill, the pair combining to toss nine scoreless innings and secure two saves against San Diego. DL Hall, Anthonio Senzatela, and Abner Uribe might not strike out ten-percent of batters they faced but the three held San Diego scoreless across 7.2 combined innings. The unit as a whole is a ground ball generating machine facing a Dodgers team that posted the third-lowest ground ball rate in the majors.

articles.title: Yankees Fan Reportedly Won't Be Punished Further After Interference on Volpe Fly Ball in ALDS
articles.summary: The New York Yankees fan that was ejected from the team's 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the ALDS for fan interference won't face any further punishment, according to Brendan Kuty of The Athletic.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees fan that was ejected from the team's 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the ALDS for fan interference won't face any further punishment, according to Brendan Kuty of The Athletic.

With the Yankees trailing 4-2 and a runner on first base in the bottom of the sixth inning, Anthony Volpe hit a ball to deep left field that was initially ruled a game-tying home run.

A review determined that a fan reached over the wall and caught the ball, leading to the home run getting overturned to a double. Meanwhile, the fan was escorted out of Yankee Stadium.

New York still recorded one run on the play, but wasn't able to tie the contest after Spencer Jones struck out to end the inning.

A source told Kuty that the fan's actions "didn't rise nearly to the level" of the two Yankees fans that received an indefinite ban from all MLB stadiums after grabbing Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts' wrist and glove during the 2024 World Series.

With New York's Game 3 defeat at the hands of Tampa Bay on Wednesday night, the Bronx Bombers were swept out of the postseason.

articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians will meet in the ALCS.

Cleveland confirmed the matchup on Saturday night with a win over the Chicago White Sox.

Jose Ramirez and Co. came back from 0-2 in the ALDS series to beat their divisional rival and advance to the next round.

Tampa Bay's waited for three days to learn its opponent in the ALCS. The Rays swept the New York Yankees in an all-AL East matchup in the ALDS.

The ALCS begins Monday night in Tampa. The Rays have their pitching rotation set the way the want, while the Guardians have some decisions to do since Gavin Williams pitched on Saturday night.

Game 1: Monday, October 12 at Tampa Bay (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 2: Tuesday, October 13 at Tampa Bay (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 3: Thursday, October 15 at Cleveland (6 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 4: Friday, October 16 at Cleveland (6 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 5 (if necessary): Saturday, October 17 at Cleveland (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 6 (if necessary): Monday, October 19 at Tampa Bay (5 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 7 (if necessary): Tuesday, October 20 at Tampa Bay (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

The Rays come into the series with three extra days of rest over the Guardians.

That allowed the Rays to reset their rotation for the start of the ALCS on Monday.

Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta should start in that order in Games 1 and 2 at Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay's pitchers kept the Cleveland bats at bay across their six regular-season meetings.

The Rays did not give up more than three earned runs in any of the six regular-season meetings between April and July. The Guardians were shutout in three of those games, including twice in the late July series.

Rasmussen struck out nine batters over seven innings in the one shutout. Nick Martinez pitched six scoreless innings in the other July shutout.

Tampa Bay's offense didn't exactly come alive in most of those games. It scored more than three runs once, but it didn't have to run up the score in games in which its pitchers controlled the score.

If the Rays pitch at a similar level, a return to the World Series should be in the cards.

Guardians Will Try To Ride Wave of Momentum From ALDS

Cleveland may not have rest on its side, but it does have the momentum gained from winning three straight games to beat the Chicago White Sox in the ALDS.

Most importantly, Jose Ramirez's bat woke up across those three wins.

Ramirez hit the game-winning home run in Game 5. He had multiple hits in Games 3 and 4, including a home run in Game 4.

The Guardians offense put up 20 runs over their three ALDS victories, a positive sign going into the brutal matchup with the Rays.

Cleveland will need a few big hits out of Ramirez and others to counter the expected big outings from the Rays.

The AL Central champion won't have Gavin Williams until likely Game 3 because he went 6.1 innings in Saturday's series clincher.

Joey Cantillo, Parker Messick, Foster Griffin and Tanner Bibee all threw in Chicago, but none of them were on the mound for more than three innings.

Two of those hurlers should be on the mound in Tampa, but that will put the Guardians at a disadvantage at least to start the series.

Williams can still pitch twice if the series goes deeper, but to start, the Guardians might have to try and extend their offensive momentum into Tampa to be competitive.

Tampa Bay won five of the six regular-season meetings with Cleveland.

The Rays pitching staff shined in most of those matchups, and the same is expected from the hurlers in the ALCS.

Tampa Bay's top arms have been difficult to hit for most of the season, so it's hard to imagine that changing now.

Cleveland can steal a win with Williams in Game 3, but it doesn't have the high-end quality in its rotation as Tampa Bay does.

articles.title: José Ramírez homers, from his shins, to complete Guardians' historic ALDS comeback over White Sox
articles.summary: It will be a Guardians-Rays ALCS after an incredible comeback by Cleveland.
articles.body: The Cleveland Guardians had to dig deep after falling behind 0-2 against the Chicago White Sox in the ALDS. José Ramírez took that literally in the Guardians' biggest moment of the season.With a two-run homer from his shins, the Guardians' longtime leader lifted his team to a 2-0 win in a winner-take-all Game 5 on Saturday in Cleveland. They will face the Tampa Bay Rays in their second ALCS in three years, with Game 1 scheduled for Monday at 8 p.m. ET.The Guardians are the first team to erase a two-game division series lead since the 2017 New York Yankees, who did it at the expense of the Guardians. That means Saturday marked the end of a charmed season for the White Sox — you could even say blessed — but few expected it to end like this.On Saturday, both teams were hitless entering the fourth inning, but Steven Kwan broke that up with a leadoff single off White Sox starter Sean Burke. Five pitches later, Ramírez broke the scoreless tie with a two-run home run at a raucous Progressive Field.Ramírez didn't just hit a homer, though. He hit a homer on a pitch that, objectively, no hitting coach would ever want a hitter to swing at, a 78-mph curveball that was destined for dirt before running into wood.JOSÉ RAMÍREZ!GUARDIANS TAKE THE FIRST LEAD OF GAME 5! pic.twitter.com/Z0zoqm513R— MLB (@MLB) October 11, 2026 Per MLB.com's Sarah Langs, Ramírez made contact with the ball 0.74 feet — or about nine inches — off the ground. That is the lowest pitch hit for a homer in a postseason game since MLB started tracking this stuff in 2008.It was a ridiculous pitch to swing at, but Ramírez has built a career on making hard contact with balls out of the zone. This time, he did it to save the Guardians' season — two days after hitting a go-ahead homer in Game 4. Perpetually underrated throughout his career, Ramírez already has a strong résumé for a plaque in Cooperstown and a statue in Cleveland. He made it even stronger on Saturday.The game wasn't a one-man effort, though. The other hero of the game was Cleveland starting pitcher Gavin Williams, who was historically dominant through the game's first five innings.His start wound up being a showcase of how quickly things can turn in the postseason, though. When Williams got the second out of the sixth inning, he hadn't allowed a hit and was up to 12 strikeouts. He was on pace for a start that would leave a mark on baseball history.All 12 of Gavin Williams' Game 5 strikeouts 😤 pic.twitter.com/m338iiKfbc— MLB (@MLB) October 11, 2026 Then White Sox catcher Kyle Teel recorded his team's first hit, which put the tying run on base, with Colson Montgomery having been hit by a pitch to lead off the inning. Then Williams walked Miguel Vargas to put the go-ahead run on base. That was it for the righty, who was pulled for left-hander Erik Sabrowski to face Chicago slugger Munetaka Murakami.In the other biggest at-bat of the night, Sabrowski struck out Murakami to leave the bases loaded and preserve Williams' brilliance. Williams' 12 strikeouts tied the Cleveland postseason record, held by Charles Nagy from his gem in the 1996 ALDS.The Cleveland bullpen had no further trouble, with Hunter Gaddis and Cade Smith combining to get the final nine outs of the game.The Guardians erase an 0-2 series deficit and advance to the ALCS! #CLINCHED(MLB x @BudweiserUSA) pic.twitter.com/g0zCsmeMPB— MLB (@MLB) October 11, 2026 It's a brutal end to Chicago's season. In a winner-take-all game, the Sox got shut down while striking out 21 times in 27 outs, with only three hits (all singles). They were 0-for-1 with runners in scoring position. Those 21 strikeouts broke a nine-inning postseason record previously held by … their 19 strikeouts in Game 3.The White Sox had all the momentum after sweeping the Houston Astros in the wild-card round and taking that 2-0 lead over Cleveland, and they were on the verge of their first ALCS appearance since their title run in 2005. Now it's over. It was a magical season, given where the Sox started, coming off a string of three consecutive 100-loss seasons after a nearly comatose decade, but this is still going to sting.

The Cleveland Guardians punched their ticket to the American League Championship Series, shutting down the Chicago White Sox in a defensive battle to clinch Game 5 on Saturday, 2-0.

The Guardians dropped both games at home before the series shifted to Chicago, where the White Sox suffered the same fate, losing both games on their home turf. With the series returning to Cleveland for Game 5, the Guardians broke the pattern, securing a pivotal victory at Rate Field.

The No. 2-seeded Guardians entered Saturday's matchup as a 1.5-point favorite, according to FanDuel Sportsbook , and delivered at home behind a dominant outing from Garrett Wilson and timely hitting from Jose Ramirez.

Ramirez broke the silence in the bottom of the fourth, launching a two-run homer that brought home Steven Kwan and gave the Guardians a 2-0 lead.

Chicago remained hitless until the sixth inning as Cleveland ace Williams dominated on the mound, racking up 12 strikeouts over 5.2 innings while allowing just one hit.

Williams was pulled in the sixth with the bases loaded and two outs, but Erik Sabrowski needed just five pitches to retire Munetaka Murakami and escape the inning unscathed.

This was not Williams' first head-turning performance this postseason. In Cleveland's 4-3 Game 2 loss to Chicago, he racked up 11 strikeouts over five innings, allowing two earned runs on four hits.

The White Sox came up clutch defensively in the bottom of the eighth, escaping a bases-loaded jam with one out after intentionally walking Ramirez. Chase DeLauter grounded into a fielder's choice, with Petey Halpin getting thrown out at home, before Jo Adell grounded out to end the threat.

Cleveland was three outs away from the ALCS when closer Cade Smith took the mound and retired all three batters in order, sealing the win and punching the Guardians' ticket to the next round.

articles.summary: Welcome, everyone, to the final four of the 2026 MLB playoffs. Otherwise known as the League Championship Series. Otherwise known as the doorstep to the World Series.
articles.body:
Welcome, everyone, to the final four of the 2026 MLB playoffs. Otherwise known as the League Championship Series. Otherwise known as the doorstep to the World Series.

In the rematch between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS, David is arguably the favorite over Goliath this time. The Brewers are cheaper my several orders of magnitude. Yet they won a league-best 103 games this year, making them the top threat to the Dodgers' shot at a rare three-peat.

It's the Cleveland Guardians vs. the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALCS, a testament to two of the best-run teams in Major League Baseball. Both have been to the World Series in the last decade, yet their respective championship droughts add up to 105 years.

So, what happens next in these to best-of-seven series?

Will the World Series be a small-market extravaganza between the Rays and Brewers? How about a 2020 grudge match between the Dodgers and Rays? Guardians and Brewers? Guardians and Dodgers?

Let's see what we can see in the form of key matchups, storylines and X-factors for each series, and then make some predictions.

Game 1 (Monday, Oct. 12): Cleveland at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 2 (Tuesday, Oct. 13): Cleveland at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 3 (Thursday, Oct. 15): Tampa Bay at Cleveland, 6:00 p.m. ET

Game 4 (Friday, Oct. 16): Tampa Bay at Cleveland, 6:00 p.m. ET

Game 5 (Saturday, Oct. 17)*: Tampa Bay at Cleveland, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 6 (Monday, Oct. 19)*: Cleveland at Tampa Bay, 5:00 p.m. ET

Game 7 (Tuesday, Oct. 20)*: Cleveland at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET

It's not a given that we'll see these two face off against each other during the ALCS. Williams just pitched the Guardians over the Chicago White Sox in Game 5 of the ALDS on Saturday. Rasmussen last pitched on October 3, so he's sure to have the ball for the Rays in ALCS Game 1 on Monday.

Even so, these two right arms will rightfully be in the spotlight after what each did in the ALDS. Rasmussen's only start against the New York Yankees was an eight-inning, 10-strikeout gem. Williams tallied 11.2 innings against the White Sox and fanned 24 batters, the second-most all-time for a single Division Series.

Adell has only played 24 games against the Rays in his career, which is about the kind of sample size you'd expect from a guy who has thus far spent his time in the AL West and AL Central.

In the last four seasons, though, Adell's 20 games against the Rays have yielded seven home runs and a .994 OPS. Somehow, some way, he's had their number.

The Rays like to run. Like, a lot. They stole 164 bases during the regular season, two more than the Brewers for the most of any team to qualify for this year's playoff field.

The Guardians only got a 17 CS% from their catchers, next to a league average of 23 percent. Yet since Patrick Bailey (32.1 CS%) was much better than Austin Hedges (6.7 CS%), they do have an ace up their sleeve if they want to make neutralizing the Rays' running game a priority.

Guardians relievers were downright nasty during the regular season, posting a collective 26.5 K% that led all bullpens. There was more where that came from during the DS against the White Sox, with Cleveland relievers racking up a 36.4 K%.

Even for a team that makes as much contact as the Rays, facing this bullpen is a tall order. They also middle-of-the-pack against relievers in general this year, ranking 14 with a .713 OPS.

The Biggest Storyline: Do the Guardians Have an Upset in Them?

Truth be told, the Guardians are probably better suited to knock off the Rays than the Yankees ever were.

The Rays play a style of clean, smart baseball that just isn't at all like the baseball that the Yankees play, and that was the latter's undoing in the ALDS. The Guardians are much more of a Rays-style team, particularly in the sense that they play good defense and run the bases well.

Yet when it comes down to it, the Rays won 98 games in arguably baseball's best division and the Guardians won just 85 games in one of baseball's weakest divisions. Even a match of like-minded teams can still be a mismatch.

At 55-26, the Rays were by far the best home team in the American League during the regular season. Yet at 44-37, the Guardians pulled off the impressive feat of being a better team on the road than they were at home.

So far, both clubs are sticking to the script. The Rays won both their games at Tropicana Field in the DS. Likewise, the Guardians won both their games away from Progressive Field in the DS.

Where's the Guardians' Help for José Ramírez?

The Guardians badly needed J-Ram to show up in the ALDS, and he did in a big way. After carrying over the silence that pervaded much of his regular season in Games 1, 2 and 3, he homered in Games 4 and 5 to rally his team over the White Sox.

Yet the Guardians only got one other homer in the series, a pinch-hit shot by Patrick Bailey in Game 4. Whether it's Jo Adell or someone else, Cleveland may not be so lucky to survive if another power bat doesn't arise to help out Ramírez.

On paper, Caminero will be the best hitter on either side in this series. He's topped 40 home runs in each of the last two seasons, with this year also seeing him up his OBP by 49 points relative to 2025.

He has, however, cooled off of late. His .772 OPS in September was his lowest for any month all season, and he was 3-for-10 without a homer in the ALDS against the Yankees.

The only forecast one feels truly comfortable making for the ALCS is that it is likely to be a low-scoring series.

Neither the Guardians nor the Rays have a high-powered offense, and literally so if we're specifically talking about home runs. The Rays hit 169 home runs this year. The Guardians, 162. Both clubs more so thrived on pitching, with each finishing the season with an ERA in the 3.70 range.

Yet if it's ultimately a question of which team can do more on the margins, the right answer simply has to be the Rays.

They're not going to give Guardians hitters any extra outs on defense, and they're going to take as many feet as they can on the basepaths. In what figures to be more of a small-ball style of series than most in these times, it's these things that will land the Rays in their third ever World Series.

Game 1 (Sunday, Oct. 11): Los Angeles at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 2 (Monday, Oct. 12): Los Angeles at Milwaukee, 5:00 p.m. ET

Game 3 (Wednesday, Oct. 14): Milwaukee at Los Angeles, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 4 (Thursday, Oct. 15): Milwaukee at Los Angeles, 9:00 p.m. ET

Game 5 (Friday, Oct. 16)*: Milwaukee at Los Angeles, 9:00 p.m. ET

Game 6 (Sunday, Oct. 18)*: Los Angeles at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Game 7 (Monday, Oct. 19)*: Los Angeles at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET

Milwaukee's catcher has had it out for Dodgers pitchers over the last three seasons, with 18 games yielding five home runs, 11 RBI and a .895 OPS. He had two games against this year in which he had multiple hits and a home run, which isn't bad for just a six-game sample size.

Perhaps more to the point, he's coming into the NLCS hot. While the spotlight was more so on Jackson Chourio, Contreras was 6-for-16 with two homers in the NLDS against the San Diego Padres.

We swear we're not doing a bit by turning the page from Milwaukee's catcher just to focus on LA's catcher. Smith has likewise been a pain in the Brewers' butt in recent seasons, with seven homers and 12 RBI against them in 17 games dating back to 2023.

Unlike Contreras, Smith was quiet in the Dodgers' NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, going 1-for-16 with seven strikeouts. With the rest of the lineup looking slightly fritzy, him living up to his recent Brewers domination would be huge.

Brewers' Small Power vs. Dodgers' Big Power

The Brewers barely out-homered the Padres in an NLDS that ultimately wasn't really about homers. They had just three to San Diego's two, for which it helped that Garrett Mitchell robbed one from Manny Machado in the clincher.

The Dodgers are going to be more of a challenge in this respect. Whereas the Padres out-homered Milwaukee by 29 during the regular season, the Dodgers bested them by 50 in the home run column.

Milwaukee hurlers threw 64 pitches of at least 100 mph in the NLDS, the most of any team for the round. And it wasn't all Jacob Misiorowski, as Trevor Megill, Aaron Ashby, Abner Uribe and Antonio Senzatela got in on it, too.

During the regular season, the Dodgers hit 100 mph better than most. Yet we're still only talking a .230 average, which isn't so much an advantage as not-a-weakness.

The Biggest Storyline: Is Revenge on Offer?

The Brewers and Dodgers first met in the playoffs for the 2018 NLCS, which saw the two clubs split the first six games. Ever since then, the Dodgers have won seven straight against Milwaukee in the postseason.

The freshest wound for the Brewers is also the big one. They looked totally outmatched in last year's NLCS, scoring just one run in all four games as they were swept. Shohei Ohtani might as well have literally kicked them out of October .

The Brewers surely want revenge. The Dodgers surely want a three-peat. Only one team can get what it wants.

No, this is not a copy-and-paste error. The Brewers went 55-26 at American Family Field, the best home record in MLB. The Dodgers went 49-32 away from Dodger Stadium, the best road record in MLB.

This is more like poetry for Guardians-Rays in that it rhymes, including with this part: Just as Milwaukee has yet to lose at home in these playoffs, the Dodgers have yet to lose on the road.

Shohei, are you there? Can you hear us? At least blink if you plan on doing something in the NLCS.

Apologies for the snark, but it is wild how much of a non-factor Ohtani has been for the last few weeks. He hasn't homered since August 18, and he was only 2-for-13 with two singles in the NLDS. He's nominally healthy, but he just isn't hitting like he is.

How good were Brewers relievers in the NLDS? Well, they recorded all three of the team's wins and allowed just three runs in 19.0 innings.

That was with just 16 strikeouts, against 11 hits and eight walks plus near-homers by Manny Machado and Ty France. So yeah, maybe a bit of luck was involved. But if it continues, just ask the Brewers if they care.

This was the same pick I made going into the Division Series round, you see. If you admire nothing else about this pick, please admire my willingness to stick to my guns.

It is an admittedly irrational pick on account of how A) the Dodgers are so much more powerful than the Brewers and B) arguably at least as good on the mound. Even if they lose the series, the over/under on how many games they'll win is around 2.5.

There's nonetheless a decent chance that this ends up being a low-scoring series, in which case the Brewers will have multiple advantages. Notably, they run the bases and field the ball better than the Dodgers do. They make things happen, and stop things from happening to them.

Also, as I said the last time: When making predictions, sometimes it's better to try to be interesting than to try to be right .

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Guardians complete ALDS comeback over White Sox, strike out record 21 batters to set up date with Rays
articles.summary: Jose Ramirez's historic low home run and a record 21 strikeouts powered the Cleveland Guardians past the Chicago White Sox in ALDS Game 5.
articles.body: No air conditioning is needed in Cleveland on Saturday night, because they are feeling the breeze of the Chicago White Sox bats. Guardians pitchers combined to strike out a nine-inning postseason record 21 White Sox batters, as they completed the comeback from down 2-0 in the American League Division Series to win Game 5, 2-0. Gavin Williams got the start for Cleveland and dominated from the jump - of the 21 batters he faced, 12 of them went down on strikes. He tossed 5.2 scoreless innings, allowing just one hit, two walks, and a hit batsman. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Williams was shoving all night, but Jose Ramirez gave him quite a nice cushion, golfing a two-run home run in the fourth inning. The pitch was 8.88 inches off the ground, the lowest for a postseason home run since at least 2008 and the lowest of Ramirez's career. That was all the Guardians needed, as Williams got five more outs, and the bullpen took care of the rest. Erik Sabrowski, Evan Gaddis, and Cade Smith combined to get the final 10 outs, striking out nine in the process (Sabrowski struck out the lone batter he faced, and Gaddis and Smith each punched out eight batters). AARON JUDGE'S FRUSTRATION WITH YANKEES IS UNDERSTANDABLE, BUT HIS 'ALL-IN' CRITICISM MISSES THE MARK Ramirez is a hero after what had been quite the down season. His .235 average, .320 on-base percentage, and .368 slugging percentage were all his lowest marks since 2015 when he was spending some of his time in Triple-A. He started out 0-for-6 in the series but went 5-for-12 in the final three, with two homers, a triple, and a double. The White Sox have been prone to the strikeout all season long, having the fifth-highest strikeout rate in the league, but this was another level. In the regular season, they struck out 24.1% of the time, but that number bumped up to 63.6% on Saturday. Cleveland lost the first two games of the series on their own home field, giving the White Sox a chance to clinch a series at home for the first time since 1906. But alas, they will now be headed home after Cleveland won three-consecutive elimination games. The Guardians will face the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Championship Series, their second trip to the round in the last three seasons. The Rays are fresh off a sweep over their AL East rival New York Yankees. articles.title: White Sox break their own 3-day old MLB postseason record with 21 strikeouts in season-ending loss to Guardians
articles.summary: Two different players in the Chicago lineup posted golden sombreros.
articles.body:
There were a lot of ways a magical Chicago White Sox season could have ended. This would be one of the worse ones.

Previously riding the high of a wild-card sweep of the Houston Astros and a 2-0 lead over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALDS, the White Sox crashed out of the playoffs on Saturday with a 2-0 loss in Game 5 . They not only choked, they choked against a division rival they were taunting via music earlier this week .

Game 5 was no normal loss either. The White Sox were shutout, with José Ramírez's homer producing the only two runs of the game. Collectively, Chicago went 3-for-30 at the plate with no extra-base hits.

In a number that defies belief, 78% of the White Sox outs came via strikeouts. Munetaka Murakami and Andrew Benintendi — their No. 4 and 5 hitters and their two highest-paid position players — both posted golden sombreros: 0-for-4 with 4 strikeouts. Four other hitters struck out multiple times.

That total is an MLB postseason record for a nine-inning game (the 1996 Baltimore Orioles hold the overall record with 23 strikeouts in 12 innings, also against Cleveland).

It also breaks a record held by … the White Sox on Wednesday, when they struck out 19 times in Game 3. To reiterate: the White Sox, on the verge of a series win, posted the two games with the most strikeouts in regulation in the history of the MLB playoffs. This team was strikeout-prone in the regular season — with shortstop Colson Montgomery setting the MLB single-season record with 227 — and that tendency bit them hard this series.

In total, the White Sox broke the record for most strikeouts in a best-of-five series with 75, breaking the previous record of 64, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs . Had this been a seven-game series, they almost certainly would have broken the overall record for a series, which is 82.

Plenty of credit is due, of course, to the Guardians pitching staff, particularly in Game 5. Starting pitcher Gavin Williams was untouchable for five innings, allowing his first hit in the sixth inning. By that point, he was up to 12 strikeouts.

Erik Sabrowski entered and defused the biggest threat of the game with a bases-loaded strikeout of Murakami. Hunter Gaddis took over from there and got all four of his outs via strikeouts. Then Cade Smith posted a five-out save, with four more strikeouts.

The Guardians used their best on Saturday, and it shows not only in the box score but in the record book. And now they'll square off against another top pitching staff in the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALCS.

articles.title: Down, But Never Out: Guardians Vanquish White Sox in ALDS
articles.summary: Cleveland dug an improbable hole to climb out of - but not an impossible one. Thanks to Gavin Williams and Jose Ramirez's Game 5 heroics, the Guardians pulle...
articles.body:
What is it about this team (and this franchise in general) and it's ability to constantly pick themselves up off the mat and keep swinging?

Externally, Cleveland was in serious trouble. They dropped the first two games of the series against the Chicago White Sox and just about everyone around the country counted them out.

Internally, I'm not sure if anyone's blood pressure even measurably raised.

Some way, somehow, this team thrives when the stakes get a little higher and the pressure ratchets up.

The Guardians pulled off a feat rarely seen in Major League Baseball - drop the first two games of a best-of-five series on your home field, then rally to win the next three in a row and move on in the playoffs.

Only the 2015 Toronto Blue Jays (ALDS vs. Texas), 2012 San Francisco Giants (NLDS vs. Cincinnati) and 2001 New York Yankees (ALDS vs. Oakland) had ever previously pulled that rabbit out of their hat.

What's even more impressive is how they flipped the switch.

Offensively, the Guards had only one base hit with a runner on base in the first two games of the series, before they exploded for 18 runs in the two games in Chicago.

Defensively, Cleveland made just one error in the entire five game series.

By the end of Saturday night's 2-0 win , the Cleveland pitching staff struck out 75 White Sox hitters through the five games in the series - shattering the MLB record they set in the 2017 ALDS against New York (64 strikeouts). They allowed an average of 3 runs and 5.8 hits per game against one of the best offenses in Major League Baseball this year.

Gavin Williams led that charge with his overwhelming performance on Saturday. Just 48 hours after coming in out of the bullpen to close out Game 4, and five days after he struck out 11 Chicago hitters in the Game 2 loss, Williams went out and pitched the game of his life. He completely suffocated the White Sox bats, to the tune of a club-postseason-record-tying 12 strikeouts over 5.2 innings. He allowed just one measly hit, walked one and hit a batter.

Cade Smith, Hunter Gaddis, and Erik Sabrowski all had a monumental impact on the Game 5 clincher as well.

The White Sox had a magnificent season and were one of MLB's all-time great feel-good stories. They lost 100 games or more each of the last three years, and turned it around to come within one win of playing in the ALCS. The Sox were one of baseball's most powerful and most patient offenses.

But they were also pretty vulnerable against Cleveland's power arms.

Consider the performances in the ALDS of Chicago's premier bats:

Andrew Benintendi, who signed the largest contract in franchise history: 0-for-7 with seven strikeouts

Munetaka Murakami, who's homer off Parker Messick in Game 1 elevated them to a win: 1-for-11 with eight strikeouts in Games 3-5

Colson Montgomery, who set the Major League single-season strikeout record this summer: 2-for-12 with eight strikeouts in Games 2-5

Miguel Vargas, who was easily the most feared hitter in the Sox lineup, broke the franchise record with 10 walks in a single postseason (let alone a series), but he never delivered a back-breaking hit that sent Cleveland spinning

All-in-all, in a game that they had to have, the White Sox swung and missed at 38 pitches in Game 5, striking out an MLB single-game postseason record 21 times.

You also can't tell the story of the ALDS without acknowledging the resurgence of Cleveland's franchise cornerstone, Jose Ramirez. Josey's resume is Cooperstown-worthy and by the time he's all done, he just might go down as the greatest player to ever don a Cleveland uniform.

But his postseason resume has certainly been lacking ... until this week.

Ramirez had been dealing with a hamate bone injury that lingered for several months, even after he got back in the lineup. But for those that weighed in on the rest vs. rust debate after the Guardians didn't play in the AL Wild Card round, consider that Jose Ramirez desperately needed that time to let his wrist/hand heal.

Everyone around that world that paid attention to this series saw exactly how important he is to the Guardians' World Series aspirations.

Who knows where this all goes. But after the Guardians went from 39-33 on June 16th to fourth place in the AL Central at 59-64 two months later, there weren't many people outside the franchise that thought they were destined for a first round bye in the playoffs ... let alone an ALCS berth.

In fact, the Guardians trailed the White Sox by 6.0 games in the division on August 16th. Since 1969, the Guardians are the first team to win division titles in back-to-back years, despite being 6.0-or-more games back of first place through at least 125 games played.

But with a flare for the dramatic in a way that only they seem to have, the Guardians closed the regular season 24-11, including a 13-5 record on the road, to surge their way to another AL Central crown.

After overcoming an 0-2 deficit in the ALDS, and certainly after watching what this core group of players has done with their backs against the wall the last three seasons, you'd be crazy to count them out against Tampa Bay.

articles.title: White Sox manager Will Venable is amazed by Chicago’s Cinderella run even in defeat
articles.summary: The Chicago White Sox’s postseason run ended one win short of the American League Championship Series, but manager Will Venable was not about to let the loss...
articles.body:
The Chicago White Sox 's postseason run ended one win short of the American League Championship Series, but manager Will Venable was not about to let the loss define what his team accomplished. Chicago fell 2-0 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 5 of the ALDS on Saturday at Progressive Field, becoming just the seventh team in the Wild Card era to lose a best-of-five series after taking a 2-0 lead.

Venable admitted the sting was real, but he also made sure to put the season in perspective.

"We are sitting in disappointment, obviously, and it hurts not to be able to advance here. That's what we came to do," Venable told reporters after the game. "So we're not just happy that we got here. We understand what it takes to get here and have more clarity on what it's gonna take the next time around to go even further."

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"At the same time, you do zoom out and you look at what this group accomplished and what they did to bring baseball back to the White Sox and the pride back to the organization and really the city," he added. "It's just amazing what these guys did."

The turnaround was stunning. Chicago lost 102 games in 2025, then swept the Houston Astros in the Wild Card Series this October for the franchise's first playoff series win since 2005. The White Sox followed that by winning the first two games of the ALDS in Cleveland before the Guardians stormed back.

Guardians pitchers struck out 75 Chicago hitters across the five games , the most ever in a postseason series of that length. Gavin Williams struck out 12 over 5 2/3 scoreless innings in the clincher, and Jose Ramirez's two-run homer in the fourth accounted for all of the scoring.

For Venable, though, the lasting memory will be the people in his clubhouse.

"I told those guys after the game this is easily the most fun that I've had in all my years in Major League Baseball," Venable said. "It's because of the personalities in that room, the character of the group and how they went out there every day, fought and did things the right way."

Chicago now heads into the offseason with plenty of reason for optimism.

articles.title: Gavin Williams again etches his name in Guardians October lore with 12 strikeouts in ALDS Game 5 vs. White Sox
articles.summary: Williams tied the franchise record with a dozen strikeouts across 5 ⅔ innings in Cleveland's victory.
articles.body:
CLEVELAND — "How will Gavin Williams look?"

Of all the questions looming large leading up to ALDS Game 5 , this collective curiosity regarding the Guardians' starting pitcher was at the forefront.

A little more than 44 hours before Williams took the mound for the winner-take-all contest in Cleveland, he was in Chicago closing out Game 4. Facing elimination, the Guardians were hoping that star closer Cade Smith could collect the final six outs, even with a five-run lead. But after a clean eighth, Smith faltered in the ninth, which ushered Williams into the game for the first relief appearance of his professional career .

Williams needed just 18 pitches to retire the side and extend Cleveland's season. But this unexpected ask of the expected Game 5 starter felt like a considerable risk at the time, even factoring in that Thursday was Williams' scheduled bullpen day between starts. There was still confidence that Williams could show up and look like his usual dynamic self, but the uncertainty lingered until the 27-year-old right-hander bounced out to the bump shortly after 8 p.m. ET on Saturday.

By the time Williams walked off the mound in the sixth inning, everyone who had been wondering what he'd have in store had their answer.

In Game 5, Williams headlined a vintage winning recipe for Cleveland: a dominant starting pitching performance followed by a trio of high-leverage heroes, plus one big swing from their best player, José Ramírez. It's a formula that has carried the Guardians to great heights during this era, and this latest rendition produced a 2-0 victory over the White Sox that sent Cleveland to the ALCS against the Tampa Bay Rays .

The victory also completed an unlikely comeback, making the Guardians the first team since the 2017 Yankees to rally from down 2-0 in a best-of-five series (which happened against Cleveland).

For the second straight start, Williams had the Progressive Field press box scrambling to determine where his outing ranked in Cleveland October lore. In Game 2, Williams became just the third pitcher in franchise history to strike out 11 in a playoff start, joining Bartolo Colon in 1999 and Charles Nagy in 1996. In Game 5, Williams one-upped himself, tying Nagy's record with a dozen strikeouts across 5 ⅔ innings.

"You don't know how somebody's going to respond to the workload," manager Stephen Vogt said amid the raucous postgame celebration. "And he just kept getting better and better and better."

For five innings, Williams held the White Sox hitless. Tristan Peters drew a walk in the second to give Chicago its first baserunner, but that frame also featured three punchouts, as Munetaka Murakami and Chase Meidroth went down flailing at sweepers and Andrew Benintendi swung through a 100.7-mph four-seamer above the zone. Williams added two more strikeouts in the third as his nasty knuckle-curve made Brenton Doyle and Colson Montgomery look silly. Facing the heart of Chicago's order in the fourth, Williams caught Kyle Teel looking at the curveball and Miguel Vargas staring at a sinker. Then he unleashed a 100-mph fastball past Murakami to punctuate the frame.

The sellout crowd of 36,889 — including new Guardians minority owner and world-famous Clevelander Travis Kelce — went ballistic.

"He had everything going tonight," second baseman Travis Bazzana said afterward. "Didn't have to worry about fielding. It was just, 'strike 3, strike 3, strike 3.'"

"I've seen it at literally every single level," said Tanner Bibee, who was teammates with Williams at multiple minor-league stops as the two climbed to the big leagues after being drafted in 2021. "When he's healthy and fully ready to go, all he's done is dominate."

Early on in Game 5, there was only one problem: White Sox starter Sean Burke was in a groove, too. His stuff wasn't as sizzling as Williams', but the results were similar. Burke cruised through three perfect innings on just 34 pitches.

But in the bottom of the fourth, energized by Williams' increasing brilliance, Cleveland's top of the order broke through against Burke. After Steven Kwan led off with a single, Ramírez brought the house down with a two-run home run that can only be described as aesthetically absurd. In a 2-2 count, Burke attacked with a sharp knuckle-curve and executed it below the strike zone. But Ramirez's otherworldly bat-to-ball ability won out, as he managed to scoop the breaker practically off the dirt and lift it just over the right-field fence to put Cleveland on the board.

Given how Williams was throwing, the two-run lead might as well have been 20. Two more strikeouts in a flawless fifth brought his total to 11. Including his relief outing in Game 4, this was the seventh time Williams had faced the White Sox this season, but Chicago's swings told a different story.

"[Catcher Patrick Bailey] did a good job," Williams said postgame about the game plan to combat the familiarity. "He was reading swings the whole time. We were talking between innings — he's phenomenal back there. I think it's more props to him than me."

"Gavin's an easy game to call for," Bailey said, downplaying the credit. "There's not really a bad pitch to call. We're just trying to mix it up, try to keep guys in-between and off-balance. And he did an unbelievable job executing."

Trouble did finally arrive in the sixth. Williams hit leadoff man Montgomery with a wayward sweeper. And after he blitzed Doyle, the No. 9 hitter, with a 98-mph four-seamer for his 12th strikeout, Kyle Teel lofted a single into right field for Chicago's first hit of the game. A walk to the dangerous Vargas loaded the bases and ended Williams' night.

But Cleveland's arms were not finished racking up whiffs. Lefty Erik Sabrowski entered and struck out Murakami to strand the bases loaded. Over the final three innings, right-handers Hunter Gaddis and Cade Smith combined to strike out eight more White Sox hitters. That brought the Game 5 punchout total to 21, a postseason record for a nine-inning game .

The previous record? Nineteen, set by these same Guardians against these same White Sox three days ago in Game 3 . And 21 isn't just a new benchmark for October; it's the most K's in any nine-inning game in major-league history, surpassing the longstanding record of 20 achieved 10 times (most recently by the Brewers against the White Sox earlier this season ).

In total, the White Sox struck out a whopping 75 times in this series, smashing the previous division series record held by, interestingly enough, those 2017 Yankees (64). Williams accounted for 24 on his own, the second-most by a pitcher in a best-of-five postseason series behind only Gerrit Cole in the 2019 ALDS (25).

These staggering strikeout totals and the lack of pitching depth that reared its ugly head in Games 3 and 4 combined to be Chicago's undoing in this series. In the end, the ALDS reflected what happened between these two teams in the regular season. Just as the White Sox let the division slip away to the Guardians in September, they were unable to capitalize on a 2-0 series lead over their Midwest rivals in October.

Of course, that Chicago was even playing on Oct. 11 is a massive organizational victory, considering the franchise's recent history, but squandering a series in this fashion undoubtedly still stings.

As for the Guardians, the show goes on. A quick turnaround is on deck before the ALCS begins on Monday at Tropicana Field . A tougher task awaits in the Rays, who present a completely different genre of challenge than the whiff-happy White Sox. Cleveland shouldn't expect to set any strikeout records in the next round.

But whenever Williams takes the mound again, the Guardians are going to feel pretty good.
