articles.title: Guardians' Sabrowski Lost His Voice Striking Out Munetaka Murakami with Bases Loaded vs. White Sox
articles.summary: Erik Sabrowski faced one batter during the Cleveland Guardians' 2-0 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Saturday's decisive Game 5 of their American League Division Series.
articles.body:
Erik Sabrowski faced one batter during the Cleveland Guardians' 2-0 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Saturday's decisive Game 5 of their American League Division Series.

And all he did was record arguably the most important out of the entire series and lose his voice in the process.

Zack Meisel of The Athletic reported Sabrowski could only talk with a "hoarse voice" after the win because "he unleashed a primal scream after striking out Munetaka Murakami with the bases loaded in the sixth."

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

The southpaw was trying to yell that Cleveland should "build a f----ng statue" with that voice when talking about José Ramírez, who launched a two-run homer in the fourth for what proved to be the game's only scoring.

Ramírez also hit a home run during the Guardians' Game 4 win in Chicago to keep their season alive and is a franchise icon at this point in his 14th season with the team.

But his home run wouldn't have been enough if it wasn't for Sabrowski's key strikeout. He entered the game in the top of the sixth inning for starter Gavin Williams with the bases loaded and two outs and struck out Chicago's leading home-run hitter in Murakami.

That was the end of his day, as Hunter Gaddis entered for Cleveland in the top of the seventh before Cade Smith eventually took over for the save.

Next up for Cleveland is the American League Championship Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, where it will need Sabrowski for more critical moments against left-handed hitters such as Jonathan Aranda and Liam Hicks.

And it will need him whether he has a voice or not.

articles.title: Wild Stat on How Dodgers' Payroll Compares to Brewers, Rays and Guardians amid World Series Bracket
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers are Major League Baseball's second-highest-spending team, and that is even more apparent when comparing them to the other teams remaining in the MLB playoffs.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are Major League Baseball's second-highest-spending team, and that is even more apparent when comparing them to the other teams remaining in the MLB playoffs.

According to Talkin' Baseball, the Dodgers' $339 million payroll is higher than those of the Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians combined:

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

The Dodgers will continue their pursuit of a third consecutive World Series title Sunday night when they go on the road for Game 1 of the National League Championship Series against the Brewers.

In recent years, the Dodgers have become known for handing out massive contracts to stars such as Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Kyle Tucker and a host of others.

Those free-spending ways have worked in their favor thus far, as they have won back-to-back World Series and are in the NLCS for the third straight year.

However, the Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing that there is more than one way to succeed in MLB.

Per Spotrac , Milwaukee is 19th in payroll at just over $146 million, while Tampa is 28th at $95.6 million and Cleveland is last at $74.4 million.

All of those teams knocked off higher-spending organizations in the National League and American League Division Series.

The Brewers beat the San Diego Padres (ninth in payroll), the Rays defeated the New York Yankees (third in payroll) and the Guardians took down the Chicago White Sox (24th in payroll).

Making it this far is an accomplishment for those teams given their limited resources compared to others, but whether they can end the Dodgers' run for a three-peat remains to be seen.

It starts with the Brewers, who had the best record in MLB this season at 103-59, meaning they have home-field advantage over the Dodgers for the NLCS.

The ALCS between the lowest and third-lowest-spending teams in baseball will kick off Monday when the Rays host the Guardians for Game 1.

Major League Baseball announced the umpire crews for the 2026 American League and National League Championship Series on Sunday.

According to the Associated Press , Bill Miller will be the crew chief for the ALCS between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, while Mark Wegner will serve as the crew chief for the NLCS between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers.

Miller will be joined by Jordan Baker, Nestor Ceja, Chad Fairchild, Adam Hamari, Mark Ripperger and Carlos Torres, while Wegner's crew is made up of Ryan Additon, Edwin Moscoso, Alan Porter, David Rackley, Chris Segal and John Tumpane.

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

Per the AP, the 59-year-old Miller will umpire the 10th LCS of his career, which is tied for the third-most in MLB history. His 126 career playoff games umpired is also second among active umps and fifth on the all-time list.

Wegner, 54, is set to work his sixth LCS after serving as the crew chief during last year's World Series.

Game 1 of the NLCS on Sunday night in Milwaukee will feature Moscoso behind the plate, while Ceja will be the home-plate umpire for Game 1 of the ALCS on Monday night in St. Petersburg, Florida.

articles.title: Guardians vs. Rays ALCS preview: Can José Ramírez and Co. keep rolling against No. 1 seed Tampa Bay?
articles.summary: The ALCS begins Monday with a trip to the World Series on the line.
articles.body:
Just as the Nos. 1 and 2 seeds emerged from the NL side of the playoff bracket , the top two American League teams also advanced to the league championship series. It's the No. 2 Cleveland Guardians vs. the No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays in the ALCS.

This will be the third time Tampa Bay and Cleveland have faced off in October. In 2013, the Rays won the wild-card game 4-0 at Progressive Field. In 2022, the Guardians prevailed in the best-of-three wild-card series, completing a two-game sweep punctuated by a walk-off home run from Oscar Gonzalez in the 15th inning of Game 2. In 2026, a best-of-seven awaits with a trip to the World Series on the line.

Game 1 is slated for 8 p.m. ET Monday at Tropicana Field . Here's a look at how these two clubs match up.

Guardians: After chasing down the White Sox to seize the AL Central title in September, Cleveland enjoyed a similar sequence in the ALDS. The Guardians rallied back from down 0-2 in the series, becoming the first team to do so in a best-of-five since the 2017 Yankees. The Guardians' shutout victory in Game 5, which featured a major-league-record 21 strikeouts and a big swing from José Ramírez , was especially invigorating after Cleveland dropped the first two games of the series at home. The Guardians then had to regroup quickly and head to Tampa to take on a rested Rays club that dominated Cleveland in the regular season, winning five of six contests by a combined score of 20-8.

Rays: Despite minimal hype entering the season — FanGraphs projected 81 wins, and the Vegas over/under was 77.5 — Tampa Bay quickly floated to the top of the mediocre American League and cruised rather comfortably to the AL East title and the top seed on that side of the bracket, winning 98 games. The Rays completed a whopping 16 series sweeps during the regular season — the most of any team in the majors — so it should have come as no surprise that once they arrived in October, they dispatched the division-rival Yankees in three games without much trouble. That means they'll be well-rested and back at Tropicana Field to begin the best-of-seven championship series, and that advantage could prove significant, considering how dominant the Rays were at home this season; their 55-26 home record was tied with Milwaukee for the best in the majors.

The terrific rookie southpaw completed five innings in 30 of his 32 starts during the regular season, and one of the two in which he didn't was his final outing in Game 162 after Cleveland had clinched. But Messick failed to go five in his first two career postseason starts and was uncharacteristically wild in his ALDS Game 4 outing , walking four batters for just the second time all season. That is not a trend the Guardians can afford to continue, given how taxed the bullpen was in the previous round (in part due to Messick's abbreviated outings); Messick will need to look more like his regular-season self to put the Guardians in position to succeed. Adding to the intrigue: Messick grew up a Rays fan in Plant City, about an hour east of Tropicana Field, and delivered one of his best starts of the season at the dome in July, throwing 7 ⅔ innings of one-run ball.

Because the Rays' pitching staff was able to keep the Yankees' bats so quiet, Tampa Bay didn't require an outlier showing from its lineup to advance, and the biggest swings of the series came from less-heralded hitters such as Victor Mesa Jr., Richie Palacios and Ryan Vilade. While the Rays' three biggest bats — Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda — all notched multiple hits last round, catcher Liam Hicks collected only one knock across his 10 at-bats. Hicks has been a brilliant addition since coming over from Miami at the trade deadline, and he has slotted in as Tampa Bay's primary cleanup hitter against right-handed pitching. His spot in the batting order could be adjusted when facing Cleveland's variety of southpaws, but he's the kind of on-base and run-producing threat that could elevate this Rays lineup from good to great if he heats up.

Full-season statistics indicate that Cleveland entered the playoffs with the weakest offense in the field (26th in OPS), but the Guardians did swing the bats well in September, lending optimism that they could produce enough run support for their sterling pitching to make some noise in October. The ALDS put both versions of the Guardians' offense on display, with largely lifeless showings in the three home games but nine runs apiece in the two games in Chicago. The difference in the decisive Game 5 was a memorable swing from face of the franchise Ramírez.

This was a welcome resurgence from Ramírez. A midseason hamate injury hampered his availability and impact for much of the summer, but his crucial homers in Games 4 and 5 marked the first time in his career that Ramirez went deep in consecutive postseason games. Talent-wise, Cleveland matches up reasonably well with Tampa Bay on the mound, but its best chance to keep pace on offense features Ramírez coming through as an all-around game-changer.

Rays: Follow the proven recipe (and their best players) to the Fall Classic

Manager Kevin Cash — the longest-tenured manager in the majors for a reason — has been pushing the right buttons all season, deftly deploying his deep roster to great effect with the help of Tampa Bay's biggest stars. That latter element will become more crucial as the Rays go deeper into October. Because as great as it was to get big-time swings from role players last round, it's only a matter of time before AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero makes his presence felt.

Scheduled Game 1 starter Drew Rasmussen also seems to be peaking in the postseason, given his dominance against New York , and the Rays would be well served if top trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta follows suit. At the same time, the Rays shouldn't have to do anything drastically different to advance to the franchise's third Fall Classic; rather, they should continue to lean on the pieces that got them this far. A slight uptick in production across the board could put them in position to give whoever comes out of the National League a fair fight.

Cleveland asked an absolute ton from its pitching staff in the ALDS. Gavin Williams made an emergency relief appearance between his two brilliant starts. Top righty bullpen arms Cade Smith and Hunter Gaddis pitched in all five games. Three other relievers — Erik Sabrowski, Tim Herrin and Shawn Armstrong — appeared in at least three. The bye week might have prepared them to handle that workload against Chicago, but there's no such break before they take on Tampa Bay, and the Rays' offense is built completely differently than the whiff-happy White Sox lineup that struck out at a record-setting rate .

In fact, Tampa Bay's hitters had the highest contact rate and lowest strikeout rate in the majors this year, a taxing trait that could exhaust Guardians pitching even further. Cleveland's offense is also susceptible to going quiet for prolonged stretches, so even if the pitching shines again, more frustrating, narrow losses could be in store.

Rays: They lose the small-ball battle and struggle in the middle innings

After toppling a Yankees team that represented an extreme contrast in style of play and roster construction, Tampa Bay is now tasked with taking down a more similar opponent. Even with a prolific power source in Caminero, the Rays ranked 22nd in homers, 27th in average exit velocity and 29th in hard-hit rate; the Guardians ranked 27th, 26th and 28th in those categories. But while they both lack slugging potential, there are some key differences: The Rays are far more proficient at collecting hits (second in batting average; Cleveland ranked 24th), while the Guardians are more willing to draw walks and drive up pitch counts (eighth in walk rate, sixth in pitches per plate appearance; Tampa Bay ranked second and 29th).

All to say: If Cleveland can find just a few more clutch swings or timely long balls from its handful of homer threats (Ramirez, Jo Adell, Chase DeLauter) and the BABIP luck is not on Tampa Bay's side, the Guardians might have an edge. The Rays could also run into trouble if they end up leaning too heavily on the bridge between their top three starters and dynamite closer Bryan Baker. Tampa Bay's bullpen ranked 19th in ERA, 23rd in FIP and 28th in HR/9, and that weakness could be exploited if the starting pitching plans go awry.

Two years ago, the Guardians went the distance in the ALDS against a division rival and won a memorable Game 5, only to be eliminated in the ALCS by a top-seeded AL East club. Will history repeat itself? It might be trending in that direction, but there are some significant differences between the Rays team the Guardians are about to face and the Yankees club that dispatched them in 2024. Tampa Bay has been incredibly consistent all year, but it doesn't feature a trio of generational sluggers like Aaron Judge, Juan Soto and Giancarlo Stanton, all of whom did major damage against Cleveland two years ago.

This Guardians club has also added major pieces since then. Gavin Williams has blossomed into an ace , and the terrific rookie class of Messick, DeLauter and Bazzana has brightened the team's present and future. That said, it's no accident that the Rays won 13 more games than the Guardians in the regular season and looked far more comfortable in the previous round . These Guardians should be more competitive than they were in the 2024 ALCS, but the Rays still have the edge.

articles.summary: Well that was tense.
articles.body:
In a rematch of last season's NLCS, the Milwaukee Brewers opened the series with a 2-1 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1, a game that will be remembered as one of the better bullpen performances in this year's postseason.

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

Each Team's Biggest Roster Hole to Fix in Offseason ⚾

The Dodgers wasted little time getting the scoring started, as an Andy Pages' RBI single in the top of the first gave them a 1-0 lead.

But it was all Brewers—and all pitching, really—from there.

Brice Turang's solo shot in the bottom of the fourth leveled the scoring.

One inning later, Luis Lara's RBI single gave the Brewers the lead.

But Game 1 was very much about the pitching and the defense for both sides. What else would you expect when Jacob Misiorowski and Tarik Skubal each took the mound?

Credit to the Dodgers—they worked Misiorowski early and drove up his pitch count, forcing him out of the game after just 4.1 innings. The issue for L.A. was that they weren't able to solve Milwaukee's bullpen, as four different relievers held them scoreless over the final 5.2 innings.

It wasn't pretty, and there wasn't much margin for error—especially when Trevor Megill walked two batters with two outs in the bottom of the ninth and had to face Mookie Betts—but Milwaukee's pitching depth, defense and timely hitting yet again led the way. They didn't win 103 games by accident.

They'll look to make it two in a row against the Dodgers in Game 2 on Monday night at 5 p.m. ET (Fox, FS1).

articles.title: Milwaukee’s bullpen delivers as the Brewers beat the Dodgers 2-1 in NLCS opener
articles.summary: The Brewers had dropped seven consecutive postseason games against the Dodgers, including a sweep in last year’s NLCS.
articles.body: MILWAUKEE — Brice Turang homered off Tarik Skubal and Milwaukee’s bullpen shut down the Los Angeles Dodgers after Jacob Misiorowski’s taxing outing, sending the Brewers to a 2-1 victory in the NL Championship Series opener on Sunday night. Luis Lara hit a tiebreaking single off Skubal in the fifth inning as Milwaukee took Game 1 in the first NLCS matchup of 100-win teams since the Cincinnati Reds eliminated the Philadelphia Phillies in 1976. The Brewers had dropped seven consecutive postseason games against the Dodgers, including a sweep in last year’s NLCS. Game 2 is on Monday in Milwaukee. Yoshinobu Yamamoto starts for the Dodgers, and Logan Henderson takes the mound for the Brewers. Los Angeles, looking to become the first team to win three straight championships since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees, grounded into three double plays, stranded nine runners and went 1 for 6 with runners in scoring position, dropping to 2 for 22 in the playoffs. The Dodgers chased Misiorowski, the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, in the fifth inning, but they managed just two hits against four relievers. DL Hall replaced Misiorowski with a runner aboard and got Freddie Freeman to ground into a double play, sending a charge through the rollicking crowd of 42,617. Abner Uribe allowed two hits in the sixth, then struck out Andy Pages with runners on the corners for the final out of the inning. Aaron Ashby pitched two innings before Trevor Megill got three outs for the save. Kyle Tucker and pinch hitter Josue De Paula walked with two down in the ninth before Mookie Betts flied to the center-field warning track. The Brewers are among five current teams that have never won it all. The Dodgers made Misiorowski throw 35 pitches in the second inning. Pages drove in Shohei Ohtani on a grounded single into right field, and Tucker loaded the bases when he reached on a 10-pitch walk that included four foul balls. But Misiorowski limited the damage when he got Kiké Hernández to bounce into an inning-ending double play. Turang responded with a leadoff drive into the home bullpen in the fourth. It was the second career postseason homer for Turang, who went 1 for 15 with six strikeouts in last year’s NLCS. Sticking with the same brand of baseball that resulted in the majors’ best record this year, Milwaukee went ahead to stay in the fifth. Garrett Mitchell reached on a leadoff walk and advanced on rookie Cooper Pratt’s sacrifice bunt. Lara, another rookie, then grounded an RBI single into center field. The Brewers loaded the bases with two down, but Skubal escaped the jam when William Contreras flied to right. Up next Yamamoto is 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 postseason appearances. The Japanese right-hander pitched a three-hitter in a 5-1 victory at Milwaukee in Game 2 of last year’s NLCS. Henderson is making his second career postseason start. The right-hander tossed five-plus innings of two-run ball in Milwaukee’s 4-3 win over San Diego in Game 2 of their NL Division Series. He went 2-0 with a 0.75 ERA in two starts against Los Angeles this season.

articles.title: Brewers overcome Jacob Misiorowski's struggles, rally to steal NLCS Game 1 from the Dodgers
articles.summary: A big hit from Brice Turang and a shutdown bullpen performance led the way for Milwaukee in Game 1.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — The Milwaukee Brewers have known for quite some time that if they want to be the best, they have to beat the best. And one year after getting swept by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, Milwaukee came into the rematch of the National League powerhouses looking to show that it's more prepared this time around.

For the Brewers to beat the back-to-back World Series champions and reach the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982, they'd have to play a nearly flawless series, beginning with a hot start in Game 1. But in a Game 1 in which Jacob Misiorowski didn't make it through the fifth inning and Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal dominated Milwaukee's lineup the first time through the order, things looked eerily similar to last year's NLCS disappointment.

Yet in their 2-1 win over the Dodgers to open the NLCS on Sunday, the Brewers showed that they can steal a game from the jaws of defeat even when they don't play their best. And they showed that this Brewers team isn't scared of a little adversity.

"That's just Brewers baseball," left-hander DL Hall said postgame. "We've all bought into that."

Misiorowski was the Brewers' MVP this season, and the equation for Milwaukee's success in this series was always going to include winning both of the fireballer's starts. But the Dodgers made the Brewers' right-hander work on Sunday and put some doubt in that plan. L.A.'s hitters took something from the Padres' approach in the NLDS, grinding out every at-bat and running Misiorowski's pitch count into the 40s by the second inning. In fact, 15 of the 19 Dodgers hitters Misiorowski faced in Game 1 saw at least four pitches in their at-bats.

But doing what an ace has to do, "The Miz" kept the Brewers in what remained a tight ballgame, getting huge double plays in the first and second innings to limit the damage. Despite throwing just 4 1/3 innings, Misiorowski allowed only one run on an Andy Pages RBI single.

"Their approach was really good," Misiorowski said afterward. "Trying to foul stuff off of me and get me out of the ballgame and try not to go deep in the game."

Misiorowski's counterpart had a much different start to the game. Skubal was dominating Brewers hitters from the start, striking out six of the first 10 batters he faced. And as the Dodgers' left-hander was carving up Milwaukee's lineup while the Brewers' ace navigated some struggles, you could feel the tension building in the anxious crowd.

Milwaukee needed an answer. And this year, whenever the Brewers have needed a spark, they've usually gotten it.

In Game 1, Brewers second baseman Brice Turang was the one to help turn things back in his team's favor. Turang's impact started defensively, as he made three strong plays to help Misiorowski get out of trouble.

And after using his glove to provide an instant impact, Milwaukee's second baseman came through with the big swing he'd been waiting on. Turang was able to inside-out a 95.5-mph sinker in the fourth inning, driving it into the Brewers' bullpen and tying the game 1-1. His first homer of the postseason couldn't have come at a better time.

"I didn't want to foul a ball off my knee again," Turang joked about his early swings off Skubal. "So I was like, 'I'm going to stay inside of this one.' … Just trying to stay inside of it, drive it up the middle, and sometimes less is more."

After Turang's home run, there was a collective exhale across the state of Wisconsin, but the Brewers still needed to get — and keep — a lead.

Rookie right fielder Luis Lara wasn't on the roster when the Brewers played the Dodgers last postseason. But with an opportunity to provide his own chapter to Milwaukee's Game 1 story, the rookie came up huge.

In the fifth inning, Lara ripped an RBI single up the middle, scoring Garrett Mitchell, who opened the frame with a walk, to give the Brewers a 2-1 lead. The 21-year-old's base hit ended up being the game-winner, as Milwaukee's bullpen tossed 4 2/3 shutout innings following Misiorowski's exit.

"Really, I was just looking to push the runner across," Lara said. "That was the only thing that was going through my mind. That's what I'm focused on in that moment, is just finding a way to connect, put the ball in play and find a way for the run to score."

Even when a game doesn't start their way, this Brewers team has a knack for finding a way to turn things in their favor. They've now done it on multiple occasions this postseason. Their grit and determination helped them overcome a ninth-inning deficit against baseball's best closer, Mason Miller, and walk off the Padres in Game 2 of the NLDS , and that mentality was on display once again in their Game 1 NLCS victory over the Dodgers.

Last year's Brewers probably lose a game like that in Game 1 – looking for a big hit, needing to turn the momentum and with a starter in a jam — but this year's Brewers have preached that they're different, and based on the results of this postseason, it's hard to argue with them.

"Guys are getting more experience. They're learning the game — even for me, still learning, getting experience. That's a big factor in this," Turang said. "Then not giving up when we are behind in the game and knowing that we can do it. We can make up runs.

"This group is really, really good with that, and it's part of the buy-in factor that these guys have done. It's part of learning and understanding and wanting to learn. It's really cool to see every day guys are learning, every day guys are getting better."

The 2026 Brewers have already done something they weren't able to do in last year's NLCS: Win a game against the Dodgers. Perhaps more importantly, they showed they can win even when the circumstances aren't perfect — a hallmark of a good team.

With Milwaukee now three wins away from the World Series, with confidence rising, there's no doubt that the Brewers know they are one.

articles.title: Dodgers' offense looks as rickety and vulnerable as ever as Shohei Ohtani and Co. lose NLCS Game 1 to the Brewers
articles.summary: The Dodgers have just 2 hits with runners in scoring position in this postseason.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — Shohei Ohtani got a haircut. It's not the only reason the four-time MVP doesn't quite look like himself.

Three-hundred and fifty-nine days ago, Ohtani delivered baseball's greatest ever single-game performance in NLCS Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers . Six scoreless innings and 10 strikeouts on the mound. Long balls in his first three at-bats. It was a sporting superhuman at the peak of his powers. It was remarkable. It was comprehensive. It was inarguable.

It was a long time ago. Or, at least, that's how it feels right now.

Because this Ohtani is not that Ohtani. This postseason is not that postseason. And this Dodgers club, 2-1 losers of NLCS Game 1 on Sunday , is not that Dodgers club. The Brewers, too, are meaningfully different this time around, a more talented, more experienced, more formidable foe. The gap, one year after Los Angeles dismembered Milwaukee in a four-game humiliation ritual, has definitively closed.

Sunday night provided an exhibition of that.

Unfortunately, Game 1 did not unfurl into the all-time classic pitchers' duel it could have been. Neither Jacob Misiorowski, the likely 2026 NL Cy Young, nor Tarik Skubal, the 2024 and 2025 AL Cy Young, were at their rip-roaring best.

Los Angeles' offense ground Misiorowski down in the second inning, plating a run and forcing the flame-throwing right-hander to throw 35 pitches. Only a timely, well-turned double play off Kiké Hernández's bat kept Miz and the Brewers from total disaster.

Skubal, in the early going, looked as overpowering as ever. He cruised through the first three innings, punching out six and allowing just one baserunner. But Brewers second baseman Brice Turang popped him for a solo homer in the fourth on a freakish piece of hitting . In the fifth, Milwaukee pushed the go-ahead run across via a walk, a sacrifice bunt and a single up the middle from diminutive rookie Luis Lara.

The score held from there. After chasing Misiorowski in the fifth, Los Angeles' lineup couldn't solve Milwaukee's bullpen. Four relievers combined for a scoreless final 4 2/3 innings. The Dodgers threatened in the ninth against closer Trevor Megill, but Mookie Betts flied out to center to end the threat and send 42,617 no-longer-tense Wisconsinites home happy.

"I thought we had a great plan. We executed against Misiorowski really well ...," first baseman Freddie Freeman said after the loss. "We did our job there, just didn't get the big hit tonight."

The Dodgers, despite besting Atlanta in the NLDS, haven't collected many big hits at all so far this October. They have just two knocks in 22 plate appearances with runners in scoring position. Both of those belong to Andy Pages, who punched home Los Angeles' only run on Sunday with a perfectly placed dribbler that squeaked through the right side. Postseason teams that fail to record an extra-base hit are now 5-35 since 2021. It's tough to string singles together in the regular season; it's even harder in October against a staff regularly touching triple digits.

That's why the long ball is so important and why this Dodgers offense, as currently constructed, looks as vulnerable and as rickety as ever. Mookie Betts, Will Smith and Shohei Ohtani, the Nos. 1, 3 and 4 hitters in Game 1, are a combined 8-for-53 with zero extra-base hits so far in these playoffs. Smith, who looks the most out of sorts, drew a walk on Sunday, reaching base for just the second time in October.

Asked whether he might move the struggling catcher down in the order, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts admitted that he'd thought about it but said he would stick with the status quo for now.

"It's hard because the body of work — and he just has that knack to get a hit, to get a big hit," he said. "... It's a fair question, but right now, I still like him at the top of the order."

Roberts, it's worth noting, has shown a willingness already in this postseason to drop his scuffling stars. Ohtani hit first in all but two of his regular-season starts and hit second in the others. But Roberts pushed him to the five-hole against Chris Sale last week and now has Ohtani slotted in at four. Lineup construction always gets more airtime than it deserves, but there might not be a more telling sign that things are at least somewhat amiss with Ohtani and the Dodgers.

"I think for Shohei, it's just kind of getting back to the basics, and I feel good where he's at," Roberts said before Game 1. "Certainly not 100 percent, but it's good enough. I think for me, it's just try to stay in the strike zone."

Ohtani expanded beyond the zone just once on Sunday, but his problems are about more than chase rate. The 32-year-old is physically compromised, a husk of the supernova who has terrorized hitters over the past half-decade. He is not rotating with the same force or freedom. He is less adaptable and adjustable to pitches in different parts of the zone. There's a certain passivity to his movement, like he's unwilling or unable to fully unleash the dragon. Considering his injury-marred second-half, that's reasonable.

When Ohtani strolled to the dish as the go-ahead run in the eighth inning Sunday, he did not inspire the same type of hearts-in-throats intimidation that he once conjured so regularly. The Brewers went right after the lefty-swinging DH; southpaw Aaron Ashby pumped three sinkers in the strike zone to Ohtani. The Dodgers superstar was a tick late and a tick under the third, lazily popping it up to third base.

Ohtani never even dropped his bat. Instead, he dragged the lumber all the way back to the dugout himself.

articles.title: Dodgers Rotation, Yankees Defense and 2026 MLB Playoffs Winners and Losers
articles.summary: We've reached the midpoint of Major League Baseball's 2026 postseason, with just three best-of-seven series remaining to determine whether the Los Angeles Dodgers can pull off the three-peat.
articles.body:
We've reached the midpoint of Major League Baseball's 2026 postseason, with just three best-of-seven series remaining to determine whether the Los Angeles Dodgers can pull off the three-peat.

What began as a 12-team free-for-all has already been whittled down to four, with no shortage of winners and losers along the way.

From dome-field advantage and the low-budget Davids vs. Goliaths to the Cubs' vanishing offense and the Yankees' hapless defense, let's relive the biggest developments from the first two rounds of the playoffs.

In the ninth inning of Game 1 of the NLDS between the Padres and Brewers, Ty France lifted a high fly ball to left at American Family Field.

Had it been a home run, it would've been a two-run howitzer, giving the Padres a 4-3 lead, and a likely victory in a game started by Jacob Misiorowski.

It looked as though it was going to drift foul, though, which would have meant continuing the AB with a 1-1 count.

Instead, it hit the rafters of the roof and fell harmlessly into Jackson Chourio's glove for the second out of the inning.

You could watch baseball for years without seeing a play like that, and few seemed to have any clue what the ground rule was in such a situation.

But a mere two days later, Spencer Jones lifted one a mile high to center field at Tropicana Ballpark, ricocheting off the catwalk before being caught by Victor Mesa Jr.

That one wasn't as big of a deal, as it was going to be a can of corn for Jonny DeLuca if it hadn't hit anything. Plus, it was in the second inning instead of the ninth inning.

Still, it's almost inconceivable that there were two instances in less than 48 hours in which the literal supports of the dome assisted the home team.

Poor defense has been plaguing the Yankees for years.

Top prospects show up and you would think they somehow made it through the minors without once bringing a glove to the stadium. And every once in a while, a veteran like Aaron Judge makes a fielding gaffe that costs them a World Series.

But their defense in the ALDS against Tampa Bay was a special breed of awful.

Game 2 was the complete and utter disaster. There were three errors within the first four Rays batters and two more botched grounders—one was ruled an infield hit, but it definitely should have been two errors—that contributed to a four-run fifth inning.

And while there were no official errors in Game 3, Taylor Walls' infield single in the third inning (which contributed to a later run) arguably should have been an out. It was a tough play, but José Caballero made it tough by playing that far back on a 2-1 count against a career .200 hitter who went 11-for-31 on bunts this season.

In the following inning, Ryan Vilade's home run literally would not have been a home run in any other ballpark —and 6'7" Spencer Jones should have been able to bring it back anyway.

Such is life in New York, where all the money in the world doesn't necessarily buy you defense.

Winner: (Almost) Every Team That Scores 4 Runs

During the final weekend of the regular season, there were a total of 44 games played. In 16 of those contests (36.4 percent), the losing team scored at least four runs.

Through the first 23 games played in this postseason, however, that didn't happen once.

That streak came to an end on Thursday in the back-and-forth battle between the Guardians and White Sox, but what a strange start, right?

To some extent, this is to be expected. Pitching duels are far more common than slugfests in October. Case in point, from 2021-25, there were 8.91 runs scored per regular season game compared to 8.10 during the postseason.

Yet, in each of the past two postseasons, we didn't even make it through the first day of the wild card round before at least one team lost despite scoring at least four runs. And by this point in both the 2022 and 2023 postseasons, there had been a game in which the losing team put up at least eight runs.

This year, though, four has been the magic number.

It doesn't matter whether it's Yoshinobu Yamamoto mowing down the competition for seven dominant innings or Anthony Kay recording one out before letting the bullpen take care of the remaining 26, the victors just keep finding a way to hold their opposition to three runs or fewer.

The 10 Greatest MLB Divisional Series Upsets 😮

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

Loser: Atlanta's Well-Compensated Position Players

The Atlanta Braves have three players on nine-figure contracts.

Austin Riley (four seasons into a 10-year, $212M deal) had a colossally important three-run home run in Game 1 of the wild card round against Philadelphia, but he went 0-for-13 with six strikeouts while playing every inning against the Dodgers. In both Game 1 and 4, he hit into the final out.

Matt Olson (five seasons into an 8-year, $168M deal) wasn't much better against LA, going 2-for-16 with a pair of singles and six strikeouts. He went hitless in six ABs with at least one runner on base, four of them with a runner in scoring position.

But the biggest disappointment was Ronald Acuña Jr. (final season of 8-year, $100M deal, with two club options remaining).

Acuña had a few singles, runs and stolen bases, but he went 3-for-24 during Atlanta's seven-game postseason run with neither an extra base hit nor an RBI. In fact, he has now gone 16 consecutive postseason games without batting in a single run, and not for lack of opportunity. He went 0-for-5 with runners in scoring position against the Dodgers, including a bases-loaded GIDP in the eighth inning of Game 2.

While Michael Harris II, Chris Sale and overnight celebrity Ray Kerr did everything in their power to keep this season going, Riley and Olson were underperforming and Acuña was sleeping under home plate.

Winner: Dodgers' Well-Compensated Pitching Staff

Yoshinobu Yamamoto is on a 12-year, $325M contract—and might be laughably underpaid at this point.

Blake Snell's deal is $182M for five years.

Tyler Glasnow is in the middle of a five-year, $136.5M contract.

Tarik Skubal is making $32M this season before his monstrous, long-term payday comes this winter.

And Edwin Díaz is the highest-paid closer in the sport on a three-year, $69M deal.

That's a combined AAV of just a little under $146M for five pitchers—which is more than the $134M active payroll of both ALCS teams combined, by the way.

But that quintet was worth every single penny in the NLDS against Atlanta.

Snell and Glasnow both struggled with their control, each issuing five walks in their abbreviated starts. But they kept the damage to a minimum, each allowing just one run.

Yamamoto and Snell both dominated in their quality starts, while Díaz allowed just one hit in his three scoreless innings of work.

All told, they went 24.1 innings with a 1.48 ERA and 30 strikeouts.

If you hate with every fiber of your being the Dodgers and the way they've assembled this deferred payroll juggernaut, you most certainly are not alone.

But while four aces couldn't save the Yankees and their $340M+ payroll from being swept—and while the Mets once again spent almost half a billion dollars to watch the postseason from home—this pitching staff makes the Dodgers feel as unstoppable as ever.

Both Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray pitched admirably in their starts in the wild card round against the Yankees. Each one departed with two outs in the fifth inning, having allowed one run in games that started out as pitching duels.

But then, Boston's bullpen got involved, and things went south in a hurry.

In each game, it was Erik Miller who replaced the starter. He immediately allowed a home run to Ben Rice in Game 1 and immediately gave up two singles in Game 2, with Gray getting charged for the run that scored. All told, he faced five batters and allowed four hits.

The other Red Sox reliever who appeared in both games was Alec Gamboa, and things didn't go any better for him. He did retire both batters he faced in Game 2, but only after failing to sit down any of the four Yankees he faced in Game 1.

Garrett Crochet's triumphant return to the mound was anything but. After Spencer Jones struck out but got to first on a wild pitch, Crochet allowed three straight hits, never officially recording an out.

We'll spare you the pitcher-by-pitcher rundown of the rest of the mess, but the overall line from the eight relievers was: 6.2 IP, 15 H, 15 ER, 7 BB, 5 K.

That's a 20.25 ERA, even with Aroldis Chapman fanning all three batters he faced while pitching with a 9-2 deficit in the eighth inning of Game 2.

Long before the postseason began, Michael King was probably destined for a nice big payday in free agency.

He was unable to fetch a long-term deal last winter, but after his second fully healthy and highly productive season in the span of three years, it's a near-certainty he will opt out of the two years and $58M left on his contract in pursuit of a much bigger one.

And whatever his market value was two weeks ago, it surely increased with his impressive run through San Diego's brief stay in the playoffs.

King absolutely mowed down the Cubs in Game 1 of the wild card round, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning before finally allowing a single to Nico Hoerner. He ended up going seven scoreless innings with eight strikeouts.

Then in Game 2 against the Brewers, King was perfect through 4.2 IP before allowing three hits in the span of five pitches. (That's baseball for you.) He still allowed just one run in five innings of work, putting the Padres in a great position to win that one.

Two days later in a do-or-die game with Mason Miller unavailable (paternity leave), he pitched the final two innings, preserving a one-run lead to keep San Diego alive for one more day.

All told, that's 14 innings with five hits, five walks, one run allowed and 15 strikeouts.

While not quite a "2014 Madison Bumgarner" or "2019 Stephen Strasburg" run through October, it was a real testament to what the 31-year-old ace brings to the table.

With 850 runs scored, the 2026 Chicago Cubs weren't any sort of all-time juggernaut of an offense, but they did lead the majors in scoring.

Over their final 73 games of the regular season, they scored at least 10 runs on 11 occasions and were held to either zero or one run just eight times—and never in back-to-back contests.

Pete Crow-Armstrong is going to win NL MVP, perhaps unanimously so after racking up 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases. Six other regulars in this lineup hit at least 15 home runs as the season-long question about the Cubs became: Is there enough pitching on this staff to routinely win games by a score of 7-5 in October?

In the end, though, it was a complete lack of offense that left them up a creek without a paddle.

While Nico Hoerner went 4-for-8, the rest of Chicago's lineup went 4-for-54 with no extra base hits or RBI.

He and Alex Bregman went a combined 0-for-15 with eight strikeouts as the Cubs were outscored 12-1.

This narrative will go out the window in a hurry if the Dodgers steamroll through the Brewers and whoever wins the ALCS to secure their third consecutive World Series title.

Thus far, however, it has been a fantastic postseason for the penny-pinchers—and, consequently, for the MLBPA's stance that the owners can stick their salary cap proposals where the sun don't shine.

Of the 12 teams who made the postseason, eight did so with an estimated competitive balance tax payroll of at least $230M while the other four ended up at $155M or below.

And when they've clashed, it has been bad news for the big spenders.

In the wild card round, the Chicago White Sox ($117.9M) made quick work of the Houston Astros ($234.7M). Jose Altuve did hit a solo home run for the 'Stros, but their septet of players making at least $18M this season was unable to take down a team with zero such players on its active roster.

In the NLDS, the Milwaukee Brewers ($154.7M) outlasted the San Diego Padres ($265.3M) in what was the most entertaining series of the first two rounds. The highlight of Game 4 was Garrett Mitchell—making less than $1M this season—delivering an RBI single past $25.5M Xander Bogaerts, tripling off $25M Robbie Ray and robbing $25.1M Manny Machado of a game-tying home run.

But the magnum opus for the Davids was the Tampa Bay Rays ($112.9M) sweeping the New York Yankees ($341.8M) out of the ALDS, nearly no-hitting the Bronx Bombers in Game 1 and never trailing for a moment of the series. Sure, Aaron Judge was unavailable, but it almost feels like it wasn't going to matter even if he had been at full strength.

In the first two years of the 12-team postseason format, first-round byes were nowhere near the advantage we expected them to be—especially in the National League, where both the No. 1 and No. 2 seed were immediately eliminated in the NLDS each year.

Quite a few "Rest or Rust?" articles were written in October 2023.

Since then, however, the pendulum has swung completely in the opposite direction.

Save for the No. 2 seed Phillies losing to the $445M New York Mets in 2024 and the No. 2 seed Phillies (again) losing to the $587M Los Angeles Dodgers in 2025, all of the teams with first-round byes have advanced to the LCS round over the past three seasons.

This year, the "Rest" squads went a perfect 4-for-4.

Granted, only the Tampa Bay Rays managed to do so in particularly convincing fashion.

The entire Milwaukee-San Diego series was gripping theatre. Atlanta put up a respectable fight against Los Angeles. And Cleveland had to waken José Ramírez from his season-long slumber in order to rally from a 2-0 deficit against Chicago.

They all got the job done, though, setting up the first 1s vs. 2s penultimate round of the postseason since 2018—which also featured No. 1 Milwaukee vs. No. 2 Los Angeles.

articles.title: Ranking the Top 25 MLB Trade Chips For 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: The MLB postseason field has been trimmed to four teams still vying for a World Series title in 2026, while the league's other 26 clubs have already shifted their attention to next year.
articles.body:
The MLB postseason field has been trimmed to four teams still vying for a World Series title in 2026, while the league's other 26 clubs have already shifted their attention to next year.

The upcoming free-agent market is thin behind ace Tarik Skubal, and that could mean a more active offseason of wheeling and dealing on the trade market. On the flip side, the looming CBA negotiations and expected lockout create significant uncertainty about what the offseason will even look like.

Assuming there is something resembling a traditional offseason, we've highlighted the top 25 potential trade chips that could be on the move. It's a mix of speculative trade candidates and players who have previously seen their names pop up on the rumor mill.

The likelihood that a player is traded helped narrow the list to 25 names, while remaining years of control, salary commitment and expected 2027 impact factored into where they fell in the rankings.

25. 3B Matt Chapman, San Francisco Giants (Age: 33)

Stats: 84 G, 97 OPS+, .235/.324/.368, 26 XBH (7 HR), 2.7 WAR Contract: 4 years, $100.7M remaining

While Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Jung Hoo Lee are generally viewed as unavailable or immovable, Chapman is the one high-priced veteran the Giants might be able to flip, using last year's Nolan Arenado trade as a blueprint of sorts. He had season-ending core muscle and hernia surgery in August, but is expected to be ready for the start of next season.

24. 2B Ozzie Albies, Atlanta Braves (Age: 29)

Stats: 162 G, 87 OPS+, .237/.293/.392, 50 XBH (22 HR), 1.4 WAR Contract: $7M club option for 2027

Albies has spent his entire 10-year career with the Braves, tallying 25.7 WAR while earning four All-Star selections and winning two Silver Slugger awards. The surface-level power production was there once again, but he has posted a middling 88 OPS+ and .299 on-base percentage in 1,350 plate appearances the last two years, and the Braves could be ready to move on as part of a larger retooling.

23. SP Griffin Jax, Tampa Bay Rays (Age: 31)

Stats: 34/23 G/GS, 3.53 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 116 K, 112.1 IP, 0.7 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $5.7M)

After four seasons as one of baseball's elite setup relievers, Jax moved into the Rays rotation in his first full season with Tampa Bay after coming over in a 2025 deadline deal for Taj Bradley. He had a 3.14 ERA, 1.11 WHIP and 106 strikeouts in 103.2 innings over his 23 starts, but the Rays have a habit of shopping pitchers with climbing arbitration salaries.

22. SP Michael Wacha, Kansas City Royals (Age: 35)

Stats: 32 GS, 3.32 ERA, 1.11 WHIP, 158 K, 200.2 IP, 4.3 WAR Contract: 1 year, $14M remaining, $14M club option in 2028

No one met the Royals' asking price on Wacha at the deadline, but he could be shopped more aggressively this winter as a reasonably priced veteran starter coming off an All-Star campaign. The 14-year veteran led the AL with 200.2 innings pitched, and his 4.3 WAR was a career-high mark.

21. 2B Xavier Edwards, Miami Marlins (Age: 27)

Stats: 142 G, 108 OPS+, .280/.360/.371, 29 XBH (6 HR), 3.0 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2029 ('27 projected: $3.5M)

Edwards was one of only 11 qualified hitters with a walk rate above 10 percent and a strikeout rate below 15 percent. He batted .321 with runners in scoring position, had 21 steals in 26 attempts and played a solid defensive second base after shifting over from shortstop midway through the 2025 season. The Marlins were listening to offers for him and shortstop Otto Lopez at the deadline, and given Lopez's extremely high asking price, Edwards is the more likely trade chip.

20. RP Trevor Megill, Milwaukee Brewers (Age: 32)

Stats: 63 G, 30 SV, 2.63 ERA, 0.89 WHIP, 10.1 K/9, 1.8 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $8.0M)

With a fastball that touches triple-digits and a knuckle curve that generated a 46.5 percent whiff rate, Megill was one of baseball's most dominant closers, converting 30 of 33 save chances. Over the past three seasons, he has a 2.61 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 10.4 K/9 with 81 saves in 161 appearances, and the Brewers have a history of flipping closers before they get expensive after dealing Josh Hader and Devin Williams.

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

19. SP Shane McClanahan, Tampa Bay Rays (Age: 29)

Stats: 24 GS, 3.36 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, 106 K, 118.0 IP, 1.4 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $6.6M)

The Rays only had four players with a salary above $6 million in 2026 and had the fourth-lowest payroll in the majors, so McClanahan is an obvious trade chip ahead of his final year of arbitration. The two-time All-Star pitched well in his return from a 2025 season that was lost to Tommy John surgery, and he has a 3.10 ERA, 1.11 WHIP and 562 strikeouts in 522.2 career innings.

18. SP George Kirby, Seattle Mariners (Age: 28)

Stats: 30 GS, 4.33 ERA, 1.40 WHIP, 148 K, 174.2 IP, 1.4 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2028 ('27 projected: $9.8M)

Even after dumping Luis Castillo's salary at the trade deadline, there is still a good chance the Mariners will shop one of their starting pitchers this winter in search of offensive upgrades. With two years of club control remaining and a down year in 2026, Kirby stands as the least likely of the three M's starters featured on this list, but he still carries significant value.

17. 2B Ketel Marte, Arizona Diamondbacks (Age: 32)

Stats: 141 G, 107 OPS+, .249/.316/.432, 56 XBH (22 HR), 2.5 WAR Contract: 4 years, $77.8M remaining, $11.5M player option in 2031

Marte earned 10-and-5 rights during the 2026 season, so he can veto any trade, but there was enough off-the-field turmoil to believe he might be looking for a change of scenery. Even in a down year by his standards, he was still one of the best offensive second basemen in the league.

16. SP Jacob deGrom, Texas Rangers (Age: 38)

Stats: 31 GS, 4.20 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 201 K, 162.2 IP, 1.7 WAR Contract: 1 year, $37M remaining

The Rangers reportedly approached deGrom about waiving his full no-trade clause at the deadline, but he declined. That doesn't mean he won't change his tune if the club starts retooling this offseason, and entering the final season of his five-year, $185 million deal, his contract is not the hurdle it would have been a year or two ago.

15. SS Corey Seager, Texas Rangers (Age: 32)

Stats: 102 G, 112 OPS+, .227/.312/.424, 36 XBH (20 HR), 3.2 WAR Contract: 5 years, $157.5M remaining

A $31.5 million annual salary for the next five seasons, coupled with his lengthy injury history, won't make it easy for the Rangers to move Seager. That said, he remains a star-level performer when healthy, and a thin shortstop class in free agency will shift focus to the trade market. For a team not willing to pay the steep price to acquire someone like Zach Neto or Otto Lopez, absorbing Seager's salary at a lower acquisition cost is a potential alternative.

14. 3B Isaac Paredes, Houston Astros (Age: 27)

Stats: 155 G, 127 OPS+, .262/.360/.447, 53 XBH (25 HR), 4.0 WAR Contract: $13.4M club option in 2027

The Astros are at an interesting crossroads, with a starting rotation that needs to be rebuilt, aging stars like Jose Altuve and Carlos Correa and two key bats closing in on free agency in Paredes and Jeremy Peña. A larger rebuild would make sense, but even if they just retool, Paredes remains a logical trade candidate given the infield logjam and his one remaining year of control.

13. OF Steven Kwan, Cleveland Guardians (Age: 29)

Stats: 151 G, 110 OPS+, .282/.382/.349, 27 XBH (3 HR), 5.3 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $11.3M)

Kwan was the third-highest paid player on the Guardians roster with a $7.725 million salary in 2026, and that is projected to climb well north of $10 million next season. The Guardians operate with one of the lowest payrolls in baseball, and Kwan has been a speculative trade candidate for years now. Ahead of his final year of control, flipping him would fit organizational philosophy. The emergence of Chase DeLauter and addition of Jo Adell has also improved the outfield picture in Cleveland.

12. SP Emerson Hancock, Seattle Mariners (Age: 27)

Stats: 25 GS, 3.57 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 126 K, 138.2 IP, 2.7 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2030 ('27 projected: minimum)

Viewed as the No. 6 starter in Seattle entering the year, Hancock got a shot at the Opening Day rotation when Bryce Miller was sidelined with an injury. The former No. 6 overall pick seized the opportunity, posting a 2.59 ERA in 41.2 innings over his first seven starts, and staked his claim to a rotation spot the rest of the way. His four remaining years of control make him significantly more valuable than his surface-level track record might suggest.

11. SP Reid Detmers, Los Angeles Angels (Age: 27)

Stats: 32 GS, 3.36 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 211 K, 185.0 IP, 4.2 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2028 ('27 projected: $7.5M)

Detmers put together a strong season out of the Angels bullpen in 2025 following an ugly 6.70 ERA over 17 starts the previous year, and it was enough to earn him another shot at the starting rotation. He ended up finishing in the top 10 in the American League in strikeouts (211, 4th), innings pitched (185.0, 6th) and pitcher WAR (4.2, 8th), and his value may never be higher for a team coming off a 100-loss season and long overdue for a rebuild.

10. SP Logan Gilbert, Seattle Mariners (Age: 29)

Stats: 32 GS, 3.73 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 205 K, 186.0 IP, 3.3 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $15.4M)

With little progress made in extension talks and free agency fast approaching after the 2027 season, Gilbert might be at the top of the list if the Mariners decide to cash in one of their rotation trade chips. Over the past five seasons, he has been one of baseball's most consistent starters, logging a 3.46 ERA and 1.05 WHIP while averaging 192 strikeouts and 180 innings per year.

9. SP Joe Ryan, Minnesota Twins (Age: 30)

Stats: 27 GS, 3.79 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, 159 K, 144.2 IP, 2.1 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $9.6M)

The Twins avoided arbitration with Ryan last January while also adding a $13 million mutual option for 2027 to the books. The club will almost certainly opt for a $100,000 buyout on that option in favor of a significantly lower arbitration projection, but he could eventually wind up on someone else's books if the Twins take another step toward rebuilding. They clung tightly to Byron Buxton and Ryan as building blocks a year ago, but after a 29-36 second half and a second straight losing season, bigger changes could be coming.

8. SS Jeremy Peña, Houston Astros (Age: 29)

Stats: 112 G, 124 OPS+, .277/.325/.477, 43 XBH (22 HR), 3.7 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2027 ('27 projected: $13.1M)

The moment Peña hired Scott Boras as his new agent in June 2025, the likelihood of a long-term extension prior to hitting the open market shrank considerably for the Astros. A wide-open AL West ultimately convinced the Astros to steer away from selling at the deadline, and even if they do view themselves as contenders in 2027, flipping Peña before losing him in free agency could still be on the table.

7. C William Contreras, Milwaukee Brewers (Age: 28)

Stats: 147 G, 108 OPS+, .270/.341/.417, 46 XBH (18 HR), 2.9 WAR Contract: $14.5M club option in 2027

The Brewers have made a habit of trading their star players as they approach free agency, with Josh Hader, Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta among the notable recent examples. That's enough to put Contreras in the trade chip conversation, especially if the club thinks former top prospect Jeferson Quero is a viable in-house replacement.

6. C Shea Langeliers, Athletics (Age: 28)

Stats: 106 G, 118 OPS+, .262/.328/.474, 44 XBH (23 HR), 3.4 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2028 ('27 projected: $8.7M)

Langeliers started the 2026 All-Star Game, carrying an .807 OPS and 21 home runs into the break. A torn meniscus in his right knee limited him to 20 games during the second half, but he returned for 13 games in September to help show potential suitors he is healthy. The Athletics have locked up several members of their young offensive core in recent years, but Langeliers has not been among them, and he could be the piece they flip to try to upgrade one of baseball's worst rotations.

Age: 27 Stats: 138 G, 115 OPS+, .245/.310/.529, 63 XBH (41 HR), 2.6 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2029 ('27 projected: $6.2M)

Only seven players across baseball have hit more home runs the past two seasons than the 72 slugged by Hunter Goodman, and his 41 long balls this year were tied for third on the NL leaderboard with Braves slugger Matt Olson.

He actually posted significantly better numbers on the road (.882 OPS, 25 HR) than he did at home (.791 OPS, 16 HR), so this is not a case of Coors Field inflating the numbers of an otherwise average performer. He has also developed into a serviceable defender behind the plate, though his bat will always drive his value.

After a fourth straight 100-loss season, nothing should be off the table as the Rockies explore ways to improve. The asking price will be high given his remaining control, but he might be the most impactful power bat on the market.

Age: 25 Stats: 157 G, 118 OPS+, .239/.330/.436, 63 XBH (27 HR), 5.2 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2029 ('27 projected: $9.8M)

With three straight seasons of 20 home runs, 20 steals and 5.0 WAR, Zach Neto has developed into one of the best all-around shortstops in baseball, but he rarely gets the attention he deserves playing for a franchise that has banked 11 consecutive losing seasons.

The Angels took a step toward retooling at the deadline by trading some controllable pieces, including José Soriano, Jo Adell and Ryan Zeferjahn, but they held onto their two most valuable trade chips in Neto and left-hander Reid Detmers.

The club's status as a perennial also-ran and a newfound willingness to move controllable pieces should make Neto one of the most talked about trade candidates of the winter.

Age: 28 Stats: 66 G, 38 SV, 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 16.6 K/9, 3.1 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2029 ('27 projected: $8.1M)

The Padres were toeing the line between buyers and sellers leading up to the 2026 trade deadline, and Mason Miller was talked about as one of the top players who could be on the move before the Padres committed to buying and added Casey Mize and Robbie Ray.

With Adrián Morejón and Jason Adam potentially departing in free agency, the Padres will be hesitant to deal their All-Star closer, but his value is so high they would be silly not to at least listen to offers.

It took an elite-level prospect in Leo De Vries for the Padres to pry him loose from the Athletics, and if a similar offer hits the table or a team is willing to part with a controllable starting pitcher, he could be on the move again.

Age: 26 Stats: 152 G, 127 OPS+, .261/.336/.497, 67 XBH (33 HR), 5.1 WAR Contract: Arbitration through 2028 ('27 projected: $10.2M)

The Nationals finished among the MLB leaders in runs scored (821, 3rd), home runs (210, 6th) and OPS (.744, 3rd), and a breakout offensive season from CJ Abrams helped pump up those numbers.

After posting a 109 OPS+ with 19 home runs and 31 steals during the 2025 season, he took things to another level with the first 30/30 season of his career and an impressive 106 RBI to rank fourth on the NL leaderboard.

The Nationals flipped starter MacKenzie Gore last winter while still trying to build back toward contention, and they could do the same with Abrams if the right package of talent improves their long-term outlook enough to justify moving an increasingly expensive star.

Age: 28 Stats: 107 G, 118 OPS+, .255/.345/.451, 39 XBH (20 HR), 1.9 WAR Contract: $17M club option in 2027 and 2028

A chorus of boos rained down on Ronald Acuña Jr. as he grounded out to end the seventh inning in Game 4 of the NLDS, stranding a runner on second base and bringing his playoff line to 3-for-24 with zero RBI.

Will that be his final at-bat in a Braves uniform?

The 2023 NL MVP and face of the franchise had a good-not-great 2026 season, and a quick move to scrub the Braves from his Instagram account immediately after they were eliminated from the playoffs fueled speculation a split might be on the horizon this winter.

With a pair of reasonable $17 million club options for the next two seasons, his contract adds to his value rather than subtracting as is the case with some other players on this list. The asking price will be astronomical, but the return could be one of the 10 best players in the sport if he locks in and returns to peak-level production.

articles.body:
Major League Baseball owners are proposing sweeping changes to the sport, including cutting the regular season from 162 to 154 games and allowing playoff teams to choose their opponents. The proposals come as MLB and its players' union approach another potentially contentious labor showdown, with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire December 1.

The proposals were submitted Thursday to the Major League Baseball Players Association MLBPA , and MLB later shared details on social media. While fans have responded favorably to some of the suggested changes, one playoff proposal has already drawn considerable criticism.

Under the owners' plan, the regular season would shrink by eight games beginning in 2029, coinciding with MLB's next national media agreement. The league argues that the shorter schedule would provide players with a standard day off each week, addressing concerns about the physical demands of baseball's lengthy season.

The reduced schedule would also create room to expand the Division Series from its current best-of-five format to a best-of-seven competition. That change, also targeted for 2029, would require teams to win four games, not three, to advance to the League Championship Series.

MLB Fans Blast Controversial Playoff Opponent Selection Proposal

However, the proposal generating the strongest reaction involves a more immediate postseason change.

Owners want higher-seeded playoff teams to select their opponents in both the Wild Card and Division Series, potentially beginning in 2027. The change would replace the current system of predetermined matchups with one that gives successful regular-season teams greater control over their postseason paths.

Fans wasted little time expressing their displeasure.

"The dumbest thing I have ever heard," one fan wrote on X. "Pick your opponent in WC round?????…….NO!"

"Opponents shouldn't get to choose opponents," another added. "Get that all the way out of here."

A third fan offered an even more colorful assessment, questioning the entire concept of opponent selection with an expletive-filled response.

MLB currently uses a 12-team postseason format with fixed seeding. Unlike the NFL, which adjusts matchups after its Wild Card round, baseball does not reseed teams based on which clubs advance. The proposed system would go much further by letting qualifying teams make their own selections.

Shorter MLB Season Raises Questions About Baseball's Historic Records

Reaction to the shorter regular season was noticeably less hostile.

"I agree with everything but the pick the opponent thing," one fan wrote.

Another fan used the proposal to poke fun at the Chicago Cubs and their supporters.

"Cutting it to 154 games is the first MLB proposal Cubs fans fully support," the fan joked. "8 fewer games to sit through before they miss October anyway."

A 154-game schedule would not be entirely unfamiliar to baseball historians. The American League last played that many games in 1960, while the National League kept the format through 1961. Both leagues later adopted the 162-game schedule that remains today.

However, returning to the shorter format would raise questions about statistical comparisons between eras.

"154 has been coming for a while, but it does affect record books," one fan observed, then asked whether records set during the 162-game era would need asterisks.

Reducing the schedule by eight games would also mean fewer chances for players to rack up home runs, hits, strikeouts, and other counting stats in a single season. That distinction could matter most when comparing modern performances with longstanding records.

Despite the attention surrounding scheduling and postseason changes, neither issue is expected to be the central obstacle in negotiations between owners and players.

Trump Backs MLB Salary Cap as Threat of Another Lockout Grows

MLB owners have sought a salary cap for decades, while the players' union has historically resisted efforts to establish one. The disagreement has previously contributed to one of the most damaging labor disputes in baseball history.

The 1994 players' strike canceled the World Series, the first time the championship had not been played since 1904. Owners then tried to prepare for the 1995 season with replacement players, but they eventually reached an agreement without a salary cap.

Since that confrontation, owners and players have negotiated five collective bargaining agreements, including their most recent deal in 2022.

This time, owners have a prominent supporter in President Donald Trump, who has publicly endorsed bringing a salary cap to Major League Baseball.

"If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One in June.

"Football has a salary cap. The MLB should have done it a long time ago."

Trump also criticized baseball for failing to establish a cap during previous labor negotiations.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

The president said he remains open to helping mediate negotiations between owners and players, though he has not announced any formal intervention.

With the current agreement expiring December 1, another lockout remains a significant concern. Owners are expected to impose one if the two sides fail to reach a new agreement, potentially putting preparations for the 2027 season at risk.

The MLBPA did not immediately respond to the Daily Mail's request for comment on the latest proposals.

For now, the league's proposed changes remain just that: proposals. Owners cannot unilaterally establish a new collectively bargained schedule or postseason structure without resolving the relevant negotiations with the players' union.

The immediate question is whether the two sides can agree before the current labor deal expires. Baseball fans may debate whether 154 games are better than 162, but another dispute over a salary cap could determine whether the 2027 season begins on time.

articles.title: Drew Rasmussen and the Rays look to overpower the Guardians in ALCS Game 1
articles.summary: Drew Rasmussen's dominant postseason form gives the Tampa Bay Rays a massive ALCS Game 1 edge over the Cleveland Guardians and Foster Griffin.
articles.body: There are some series you feel like are over before they even begin. I am not sure that it always works out, but there are some times when it does. This feels like a series that is more of a formality than anything. The Guardians and the Rays are playing in the American League Championship Series, and this just feels like the Guardians will be significantly overmatched. The Guardians have won three straight games, and that’s how they got into this series in the first place. They lost two games in a row to the White Sox, then they found a way to break the bats out in Games 3 and 4 in Chicago. That forced a Game 5 back in Cleveland, where their pitching was lights out and the hitting did just enough for them to secure a victory. It just feels like they aren’t nearly as good of a team as the Rays. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Monday night, they are sending out Foster Griffin to the mound. I would like to go on the record to say I thought Griffin should’ve been given a start in the Chicago series. For whatever reason, he wasn’t. He only pitched in Game 3 and allowed one earned run over 2.2 innings and struck out seven hitters. Griffin did not start that game. He is now on full rest facing the Rays to open the series. He did not face the Rays at all this season, but has faced two Rays hitters in his career, striking out Jonathan Aranda and walking Taylor Walls. GUARDIANS COMPLETE ALDS COMEBACK OVER WHITE SOX, STRIKE OUT RECORD 21 BATTERS TO SET UP DATE WITH RAYS The Tampa Bay Rays were the best team in the American League this season, and they looked like it in the Division Series against the Yankees. When they needed to stifle the Yankees’ bats, they did. When they needed a big hit, they got it. They took advantage of the defensive miscues and swept away New York. Game 2 was where the Rays found the way to make it work against a lot of questionable plays from New York. They got a major hit in Game 3. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE In Game 1, it wasn’t either of those things; it was a masterpiece thrown by tonight’s starter, Drew Rasmussen. How good was his first game? He went eight innings, walked two hitters, allowed one hit, and struck out 10 hitters without allowing a run. His season was fantastic, ending with a 16-5 record, 2.67 ERA, and a 0.91 WHIP. He faced the Guardians twice this season. On the road, he went five innings and allowed two earned runs on six hits. At home, he allowed one hit and one walk over seven scoreless frames. Not only in this series, but in this game, I think the Guardians have no chance. Sure, there could be the rest vs. rust factor. There could be a game here from the Rays where they just can’t get a hit. However, Rasmussen is a true Ace and gives the Rays a major advantage. Griffin could be a very good starter and give the Guardians a chance. I just don’t see it here. Give me the Rays on the run line. The moneyline is too juicy for me to take and I think Tampa will win by two or more. articles.title: Yoshinobu Yamamoto takes the mound as Dodgers look to even NLCS after Game 1 loss to Brewers
articles.summary: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, last year's World Series MVP, takes the mound for the Dodgers in NLCS Game 2 after Milwaukee seized home field advantage.
articles.body: There are a lot of people who will say that this series, for all intents and purposes, is the World Series. I’m sure most think whoever escapes the National League Championship Series will end up as the winner. I’m not quite sure I fit that description. I think it is possible the Rays, and maybe to a lesser extent the Guardians, could beat either of these teams, but the NL will likely have the favorite in the World Series. The Los Angeles Dodgers got to the postseason by being one of the best teams in baseball and winning the National League West. They built their team by adding pieces each year. This year in the offseason, they added a closer and the best hitter available. During the season, they added Tarik Skubal, the best pitcher potentially on the planet, and he pitched yesterday. The Dodgers have won two straight World Series and are looking for a third. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! They have a great chance to win tonight given that they are sending out last year’s World Series MVP. Yoshinobu Yamamoto seems to be one of the best postseason pitchers out there. This year he made one start, going 1-0, allowing four hits and one earned run over seven innings. He struck out 10 Braves in the 3-1 win for the Dodgers. Since he joined the Dodgers, he has pitched in 11 postseason games and the Dodgers have won 10 of them. He’s allowed 15 earned runs in 63 innings. LOS ANGELES DODGERS ARE BACK IN THE NLCS FOR THIRD STRAIGHT SEASON AFTER WIN OVER ATLANTA BRAVES The Milwaukee Brewers have gotten here without the big additions that the Dodgers get. They are a solid team that has actually traded away or let players walk that were major contributors. It hasn’t mattered; they just keep winning. This year, the team feels much more confident. The players look ready and locked in. Will that mean they can finally overcome the Dodgers? Honestly, it is hard to say. No one really matches up well with the Dodgers, but the Brewers have home field advantage, solid hitting, and a good pitching staff. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The Brewers are sending out their second-best arm to the mound today. Logan Henderson takes the ball, and he went 11-3 in the regular season with a 2.47 ERA and a 0.84 WHIP. He pitched against the Padres and allowed one earned run over five innings on two hits and three walks. He faced the Dodgers twice this year, allowing just one earned run on five hits over 12 innings of work. He struck out 13 hitters in those two games as well. In Game 1, the Dodgers struck first, but despite hitting the ball well and getting runners on base, they couldn't get more than one run. The Brewers tied the game on a home run. Then later, they got a walk, bunted, and singled home a run. That was all the scoring in the game, and it gave Milwaukee a win in the first game. I was actually encouraged by the Dodgers' bats - they didn't get the hits when needed, but they had traffic on the bases and weren't completely reliant on homers.
